I thought it interesting to make a wide and broad unassociated leap and associate but not connect some data. IPhone apps . Based on comprehensive data from industry reports and app store analytics, here are the sobering statistics about iPhone app performance since 2020:

Apps Created Since 2020

The iPhone App Store has experienced massive growth, with approximately 2.9 million new apps added since 2020. Currently, there are 1.96 million apps available for download, with an average of 1,615 new apps published daily. This represents about 45,000-51,000 new apps added monthly.

iPhone app success funnel showing the dramatic drop from 2.9 million apps created since 2020 to just 14,500 truly successful apps

Download Performance: The First Reality Check

The download statistics reveal the first major hurdle for app success:

  • 68% of all apps never reach 1,000 downloads.

  • Only about 900,000 apps (32% of those created since 2020) achieve meaningful download numbers.

  • The top 200 apps generate an average of $82,500 daily, while the top 800 generate around $3,500.

  • 77% of users abandon apps within the first 3 days

Daily Active Users: The Engagement Reality

While user engagement can be high for successful apps, most struggle to maintain meaningful daily active user numbers:

  • 49% of people open an app 11+ times per day, but this is concentrated among very few apps.

  • Users interact with an average of 10 different apps daily and 30 apps monthly.

  • Top social apps like Facebook (283 million DAU) and WhatsApp (270 million DAU) dominate engagement.

The Success Paradox

The data reveals a stark paradox in the iPhone app ecosystem:

  • Market Growth: The mobile app market reached $150 billion in consumer spending in 2024, with iOS responsible for 68% of that revenue.

  • Individual Failure: Despite the massive market, 99.5% of consumer apps fail to achieve meaningful success.

  • Revenue Concentration: The top 1% of apps capture the vast majority of revenue, while most apps generate virtually nothing.

Who Benefits from "Uber Efficiency"?

The statistics clearly show that the current app ecosystem's emphasis on rapid deployment and algorithmic optimization primarily benefits:

  1. Platform Owners (Apple): Earning billions from the 30% commission on successful apps.

  2. Top Apps: The 0.5% that achieve success capture disproportionate rewards.

  3. Development Tools/Services: Companies providing analytics, marketing, and development platforms.

Meanwhile, individual developers and small businesses face:

  • 67% never break even on their development costs.

  • Median revenue that cannot support a sustainable business.

  • Extreme competition in an oversaturated market

The Efficiency Trap

So what is my hypothesis? Let’s start with, I am not terribly smart. Behavior, en masse, tells us we are distracted, distressed and unable to create maximum or even minimal utility for the technology we already have. How on earth do we think agentic futures are what we are geared for. Maybe it is a generational thing. Maybe the Irish government have given me a signal.

These numbers suggest that the pursuit of "uber efficiency" in app development and deployment has created a system that efficiently produces failure. The ease of creating and publishing apps has led to market saturation where quality and genuine user value are drowned out by sheer volume.

Does this hyper-efficient system of rapid app creation and algorithmic distribution actually serve human needs, or does it primarily serve the platforms that profit from the volume game?

The data suggests that for most developers and users alike, the current "efficient" system may be anything but efficient at creating meaningful, sustainable digital experiences.

My own phone usage tells its own tale too. I see most family and friends the same. What am I missing.

If eBay were a character from Clueless, it would be Tai. At first glance, Tai (played by Brittany Murphy) arrives as an outsider—awkward, under-polished, and not quite fitting in with the polished tech world of Cher and Dionne (read: Amazon and Apple). But underneath that exterior lies authenticity, heart, and potential to completely transform the social order.

Just like eBay, Tai helped everyone find something they didn’t know they needed. She made it okay to be weird, to trade Pokémon cards, vintage handbags, or auto parts from your garage. She was peer-to-peer before it was cool.

As the world changes, others get glossier, faster, more algorithmic. But Tai—like eBay—still has a soul. Still believes in the power of real people doing real business.

“You know, I may not be a total Betty, but I’ve helped a lot of people get what they want—and that’s kind of major, don’t you think?”

Ebay in my nutshell is Tai Fraser.

"Do you prefer fashion victim or ensembly challenged?"Early eBay – Disrupting the Status Quo

Ebay holds this unique place in my heart which is fundamental to how I think through commerce - it’s people, processes and how fun it can be too. Working with them under CEO, Lorrie Norrington, was an immense amount of fun and privilege. Travelling and meeting customers, working in warehouses and understanding how important to many casual sellers eBay was. I was employee number 2 to ever meet a customer. I met people I call friends today and customers that I call on for help every now and again.

When I first walked into to Blanch (Dublin) to the training room, I was greeted by this value - TRUST. Everything revolved around it - still does today. With power comes responsibility and eBay has always anchored itself with this. Today it is more like a weight. eBay needs to be liberated but from what and who. Let’s look back to look forward. This

Pierre Omidyar’s vision was revolutionary—a marketplace defined by openness and honesty. His now-legendary first sale, a broken laser pointer, set the tone for eBay's early identity. By connecting niche buyers and sellers, Omidyar established the foundations of a "perfect market" driven by genuine supply and demand, challenging conventional retail models.

Today, eBay stands as a globally recognized marketplace, active in over 190 countries, boasting a cash-rich balance sheet and robust financial health. With 134 million active buyers and approximately 17.6 million active sellers, eBay maintains significant market presence, yet curiously seems absent from contemporary cultural conversations. Despite its financial stability and continued global reach, eBay has gradually slipped from the cultural zeitgeist.

Currently led by Jamie Iannone, a CEO deeply familiar with the platform’s strengths and challenges, eBay faces a critical juncture. While it remains profitable and operationally sound, the platform struggles against perceptions of stagnation in comparison to agile, innovative competitors like Amazon, MercadoLibre, and Alibaba. This stagnation, while not indicative of a failing business model, signals a risk of gradual decline into irrelevance if proactive measures are not taken.

But here is the rub. Maybe I got this all wrong. I spoke with analyst and friend Hendrik Lauscher just now and he posed so many sliding doors moments for eBay. Is it a victim of itself. Historically and currently a financially sound, not spectacular organization.

Looking forward, eBay’s leadership seeks rejuvenation through targeted innovation in technology, specifically artificial intelligence and mobile commerce enhancements, alongside strategic expansions in underpenetrated global markets. The company also emphasizes sustainability and circular economy principles—areas resonating strongly with contemporary consumer values. Whether these initiatives can revive eBay’s cultural relevance and competitive edge remains an open and crucial question for the brand’s future.

"You see how picky I am about my shoes, and they only go on my feet."Building Trust and Community: Innovations and Challenges. eBay made a samurai out of the Keyboard Warrior.

One of eBay’s landmark innovations was its feedback system, introduced in 1996. This groundbreaking approach established a foundation of trust essential for ecommerce, addressing early concerns about online transaction reliability. Buyers and sellers rated each other, creating a transparent, self-regulating community that facilitated safer and more confident transactions.

The ripple effects of this trust mechanism have profoundly influenced online commerce beyond eBay, shaping how digital marketplaces operate globally. Competitors and new ecommerce platforms frequently adopt variations of eBay’s rating model, recognizing its vital role in user confidence, retention, and engagement.

Today, however, trust online has evolved significantly. Ebay took this shit seriously though. Feedback was/is linked to a metric that is actively managed - BBE - Bad BUyer Experience - the cost to win back a customer through marketing because of a BBE. This is a metric that should be presented to every branda.

BBE proposes using feedback not only for sellers but also for buyers. Could such a feedback system serve as a guardrail against serial fraud, excessive returns, late payments in Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) schemes, and other problematic consumer behaviors?

This raises broader questions about the evolution of trust mechanisms in ecommerce:

Would implementing buyer ratings reduce fraud and improve marketplace efficiency?

How would buyer feedback impact consumer behavior?

Could this model significantly shift power dynamics, encouraging responsible consumerism?

These considerations indicate where feedback systems might lead next, extending eBay’s original innovation into new frontiers of online marketplace regulation and transparency. Could such a feedback system serve as a guardrail against serial fraud, excessive returns, late payments in Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) schemes, and other problematic consumer behaviors?

"You're a virgin who can't drive."Mean Girls talking Strategic Missteps and Perception Issues

Over the decades, eBay has engaged in a flurry of acquisitions and divestitures—some visionary, others perplexing. Strategic decisions made during periods of intense growth, executive transitions, and competitive pressure have not always aged well. The composition of the company needs to be seen to be believed. It is enormous, far reaching and innovative

Previously Owned and Divested

Top 3 Best Acquisitions/Divestments:

PayPal (Acquired 2002, Divested 2015) Arguably the smartest move eBay ever made—acquiring PayPal legitimized its payments ecosystem, increased buyer trust, and improved transaction velocity. Even though it was later spun out, PayPal’s growth post-eBay shows how integral it was to both platforms’ trajectories.

StubHub (Acquired 2007, Divested 2020) Sold to a group of touts - kidding but that would have been very funny. StubHub was eBay’s move into event-based commerce. While the $4.05B sale to Viagogo in 2020 wasn’t record-breaking by modern standards, it reflected a smart repositioning to streamline eBay's core commerce focus—especially before the pandemic decimated live events.

Gmarket (Acquired 2009)eBay’s acquisition of Korea’s Gmarket gave it a foothold in one of Asia’s most competitive e-commerce markets. It provided insight into localized platforms and gave eBay credibility in the global expansion playbook. T his one is for you

Top 3 Worst Acquisitions/Divestments:

Skype (Acquired 2005, Divested 2009)In one of the most baffling deals, eBay bought Skype for $2.6B with the hope of integrating voice into ecommerce. It never worked. The divestment to a private group including Silver Lake and Andreessen Horowitz for $1.9B was an expensive detour.At the time there was a story circulating that the then CEO mailed everyone talking about this great new investment and inf anyone knew,

“How to monetize it” to please let her know.

Magento (Acquired 2011, Spun out 2015)Magento could have been eBay’s answer to Shopify. Instead, poor integration under the eBay Enterprise umbrella led to underperformance. Adobe acquired Magento in 2018 for $1.68B—turning what could have been eBay’s platform ecosystem into Adobe’s.

eBay Enterprise (Formerly GSI Commerce)Acquired for $2.4B in 2011 and then broken up and sold for parts by 2015, this was a clear misfire. eBay never fully understood how to integrate enterprise services into a peer-to-peer marketplace. It still doesn;t and at its core, this is a problem.

These acquisitions reflected eBay's fluctuating identity—from marketplace purist to full-stack platform operator and back again. Strategic missteps weren’t always about the target but about execution and fit. Sliding doors or shifting momentum - zero consistency.

Each missed integration represented more than just financial loss—it was an erosion of strategic focus. Today, with competition accelerating and platforms scaling through vertical integration, eBay must make smarter choices that reinforce its core identity.

Struggle Bus Ep 6 Dropped: Some guests talk about ecommerce like it’s a spreadsheet. Scott Lux talks about it like it’s a song. 🎶 On our latest episode, Scott (EVP Global Ecomm & Tech at Esprit) reminded me why I started this podcast in the first place: to capture the real human side of retail and technology. Not just the KPIs, not just the jargon, but the lived experiences that shape how we show up in this industry.

Scott grew up in Dallas, Texas, in his dad’s lighting store. Before “big box,” before Home Depot, before Amazon. Just a shop on the high street where half the business was B2C (families coming in to buy lamps for their homes) and the other half was B2B (homebuilders needing fixtures for projects).

Weekends for Scott meant sweeping floors, carrying boxes out to customer cars, and watching his dad build relationships one handshake at a time. When his dad splashed out on a half-page ad in the Dallas Morning News sports section, Scott remembers seeing the family business side by side with the Dallas Mavericks , a reminder that retail is as much about belonging in culture as it is about selling.

And right across the street? A record store called Sound Warehouse. That’s where Scott discovered punk, heavy metal, and the thrill of finding music that wasn’t on FM radio. His first CD was Led Zeppelin IV.

What did we learn from Scott?

💡 That retail relationships outlast any tech stack. His dad’s lessons about knowing customers, looking after staff, and building trust still apply, whether you’re running a lighting shop in Dallas or a global fashion brand.

💡 That slowing down beats rushing ahead. Scott sees “first-mover advantage” as overrated, whether it’s AI or ecommerce tools, moving fast without purpose is just asking for injury. Like running a marathon, you have to train, grind, and embrace the bad days.

💡 That technology should enable, not replace, thinking. His contrarian take on AI is simple: it’s not that he’s against it, but he’s against outsourcing our brains. Retail is complex, but we’re the ones making it overcomplicated by chasing shortcuts.

💡 That humility matters more than ego. He leads with transparency, curiosity, and ownership. In his words: “Not every day is going to be a winner. But you put the work in, and the reward is greater when you do struggle and get through it.”

international-growth-is-sexy.html:
This post was sponsored by Avalara but the opinions are my own and don’t necessarily represent Avalara’s positions or strategies.

In Shopify’s earnings call earlier this year, they made something abundantly clear: international expansion is a strategic priority.

It’s also a compliance nightmare.

Yes, the modern ecommerce brand playbook tells us to “go global” — sell into new markets, unlock new customers, and make your brand borderless. But in 2025, doing that without a solid tax compliance strategy is like launching your store without HTTPS. Without a Growth Strategy, all of the hard work on building efficiency means nothing.

Avalara’s latest research — The State of International Ecommerce 2025 — is great bed time reading for anyone scaling beyond their domestic borders. And yes, full disclosure, I worked with them on this because being European, and specifically an Irish European person, with a big voice, I thought it fair to share..

Let me break it down as I see it.

The Promise of Global Ecommerce vs. The Reality of Tax Chaos

Here’s the good news: global ecommerce is still growing. Businesses in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Australia, and New Zealand are diving into cross-border sales— with 88% of U.S. and 94% of Canadian companies selling into other North American markets.

Here’s the bad news: 92% of tax compliance decision-makers say global tax compliance has become significantly more complex in the last two years. But then, it has always been hard. Now, our options are more limited. There are only so many more ways to say no.

Why?

Because in 2025:

  • Regulations are evolving faster than your TikTok algorithm. (That’s fast!).

  • Tariff classifications change without notice, tanking your margin. (Tariff spreadsheets are even doing the rounds in Congress)

  • Governments are using AI to flag noncompliance — and ignorance is no longer an excuse. (and we all trust AI).

  • Marketplaces and platforms are being pushed to share the liability — Shopify can’t save you from bad VAT handling.

📉 75% of companies have already felt the pain — in audits, fines, delayed shipments, or customer churn due to compliance blunders.

Top Expansion Markets Are Also Top Risk Zones

Everyone wants to tap into North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. But if you’re not up to speed on local tax rules, you’re not ready for the ride.

Take this stat: 82% of respondents said compliance challenges are moderately or significantly impacting their ability to scale internationally.

And not all markets are created equal:

  • U.S. and U.K. sellers are twice as likely to feel serious disruption from compliance issues.

  • B2C brands get hit hardest on logistics, local currency setup, and tax transparency.

  • B2B brands struggle more with jurisdictional complexity, documentation, and exemption rules.

Translation? Different playbooks for different players. One size fits nobody. I have said this before, we live in a multi tiered system. Your job is to play there - properly.

Tax Is a Tech Problem Now (Whether You Like It or Not)

This is where the research gets juicy.

Companies that use tax automation tools are:

  • Nearly 2x more likely to say they’re “very satisfied” with their compliance.

  • More confident in managing audits.

  • Less stressed when tariff codes do their monthly disappearing act.

Yet — 53% of ecommerce businesses are still not happy with their current compliance tools.

Why?

Because too many still operate in silos, manually calculating landed costs, or Googling VAT thresholds at 11 PM. Not only is that unsustainable, it’s dangerous. Hard to believe we are writing this in 2025 - read on.

🚀 In 2025, your compliance stack is your growth enabler.

Whether you're using Avalara or not, the takeaway is clear:

  • Automate tax classification and rate lookups.

  • Sync your ecommerce platform with your tax software.

  • Update your strategy monthly, not just when things go wrong.

Customer Experience = Compliance Experience

This one might surprise you — pricing transparency and local tax compliance were ranked as the top ways to improve international customer experience.

Why? Because no one likes surprise fees at checkout.If you’re trying to build trust in new markets, it starts with:

  • Showing total landed costs, upfront.

  • Complying visibly with local tax laws.

  • Offering localized returns, currency, and support.

📦 Remember: delayed shipments from misclassified goods or customs issues are not just a tax problem — they’re a retention problem. Your customers do not care about YOUR problems.

The Cost of Getting It Wrong

Not even Mary Poppins can rescue this. Let’s not sugarcoat it:

  • 43% of companies faced increased audits.

  • 42% experienced shipment delays.

  • 32% got hit with fines or penalties.

  • 25% said customer experience suffered.

These aren’t hypotheticals. These are margin killers.

The brands that fare best? They have:

  • Dedicated internal tax teams.

  • Clear processes.

  • A budget that reflects the importance of tax. (24% of confident companies invest >20% of their compliance budget in tax.)

If you're treating tax as an afterthought, your growth is built on a house of sand.

From Tools to Talent: What’s Needed Next?

The research shows a shift in focus:

  • Execs want AI-driven compliance and predictive analytics.

  • Teams on the ground want better automation, real-time alerts, and smarter filing tools.

What everyone agrees on:

  • Tech must integrate seamlessly into existing systems.

  • Automation isn’t optional anymore — it’s table stakes.

  • Knowledge-building (e.g., training, regulatory updates) is just as vital as the tools themselves.

The top three wishes from tax leaders?

  1. Seamless integration with finance tools (48%)

  2. AI-powered compliance assistance (47%)

  3. Better user experience (47%)

In short: they don’t want another dashboard. They want a co-pilot.

So What Do We Do With All This?

If you’re a Shopify brand or ecommerce operator reading this, here’s what I’d suggest:

✅ Start with a tax tech audit

Review your current stack. Are you relying on Shopify’s built-in tax settings alone? Is your tax rate data updated automatically? Are you classifying goods correctly? Are you audit-ready?

✅ Get proactive — not reactive

High-confidence companies update their strategy monthly and invest in tools that evolve with regulation. Don’t wait for a fine to justify the budget.

✅ Localize your compliance

Each region has different rules, thresholds, and enforcement priorities. Tailor your strategy per market — don’t assume U.S. norms will work in the EU or ANZ.

✅ Bring in experts

External advisors aren’t just for damage control. They’re a force multiplier, especially when paired with internal systems and automation.

Shopify Editions Summer 2025 and Shopify Earnings - Some Pause

Shopify’s Summer 2025 Editions update places a renewed emphasis on its global footprint, reflecting a clear intent to solidify its position as the preferred commerce infrastructure for international sellers. The update announces an expansion of Shopify Markets Pro to merchants in the UK, unlocking features like end-to-end international fulfillment, duties-inclusive pricing, and fully managed compliance.

Notably, Shopify now supports payments in 150+ currencies and duties/taxes calculations across 200+ countries—up from 175 countries as previously mentioned in the Q1 2025 earnings call. This indicates a tangible expansion of market coverage and functionality since Q1.

However, the Editions release does not introduce new countries outright in terms of domestic platform expansion or local payment stack rollout, which suggests Shopify may be focusing more on deepening capabilities in existing global markets than rapidly adding new ones.

From a strategic lens, the Q1 press release emphasized Shopify’s role in simplifying cross-border complexity—something the Editions update delivers on by tightening logistics, compliance, and localization for key international markets. What appears to be missing, though, is detail on any APAC-specific country entries or local partnerships—an area that remains a growth opportunity.

Shopify’s global strategy is advancing with more tools and reach for existing international merchants. The push is less about flags-on-the-map expansion and more about building a resilient infrastructure for truly global commerce.

Result? Shopify and Avalara agree.

🧩 Final Thought: Agility Wins

Shopify brands are some of the most innovative and aggressive when it comes to growth. But here’s the thing — growth without compliance is a liability.

The brands that will win international ecommerce in 2025 aren’t the biggest, or the fastest. They’re the ones who can adapt quickly, make tax seamless, and stay one step ahead of regulators without slowing down the business.

Tax may not be sexy — but avoiding a customs hold or five-figure fine? That’s hot.

Earworm alert: Cue angsty guitar riff from Liam Lynch's one-hit wonder, fade into a dystopian pop-up shop where every price tag is handwritten in five currencies, and the cashier is a chatbot named "Todd" who insists on upselling you customs duty insurance. Is better to burn out or fade away.

It’s 2025, your face serum ships from Seoul, your runners/trainers/sneakers from Sydney, and your trust in cross-border delivery from somewhere between purgatory and a DHL warehouse. In many non religions, they are the same thing. In prep for the Ostrich Report, I have been doing some reading. This time a trip to FlavorCloud. FlavorCloud's "State of Cross-Border Consumer Insights 2025" dropped like an Amazon drone into our inbox this week. Well actually Hendrik gave it to me. So here is my view on the chaotic, tariff-choked, zone-restricted world of global ecommerce—V Spot style.

And yes, it’s called My United States of Whatever. Because that’s what cross-border ecommerce looks like today: fragmented, over-legislated)not necessarily a bad thing), algorithmically priced madness where brands want growth but get spreadsheets.

The Exhausting Annual Marvelicious and Superfluous Global Tug-of-War: From Growth Strategy to Survival Mode

Pre 2020, we were the pariahs. Post 2020, we remain the pariahs. However in 2020, cross-border trade was a nice-to-have. By 2025, it’s an existential necessity, to us. Who is “us”. US is a small tribe of people who believe that cross Border trade or international, as the French Canadians call it have long since held a view that CBT will help on your growth journey. An indication of how serious you want to be perceived. So serious, that you send your canary down the mine first (your marketplace manager - who has 60% of the salary of your head of ecommerce and 5% of the budget. AnIT “resource” and an annual battle to prove marketplaces work. Enough of my flapping.

According to FlavorCloud, over 31% of global ecommerce is now cross-border, a number that sounds great until you realize it’s being choked by tariffs like a cargo ship stuck sideways in the Suez Canal. True Story.

Merchants aren’t just optimizing for speed, they’re dodging retaliatory tariffs like it’s a dodgeball game between Biden, Trudeau, and Xi Jinping. Dodge, duck, dip, dive, dodge? New tariffs in 2025? Yep. 25% extra on Canadian and Mexican goods, plus China’s revenge tax plan. And this isn't a Netflix original, it's real life.

Naomi Klein called it 20 years ago in No Logo: global brands, local casualties. Back then, the enemy was sweatshops and street protests. Now it’s Customs & Border Protection and opaque HS code classifications and em, sweatshops and street protests. The circle of life.

Health & Wellness: The New Oil (Palm free mind you so everyone’s a winner, right?)

In this strange, digitized global bazaar, one vertical has emerged as a cross-border juggernaut: Health & Wellness. But try calling someone in the space a Juggernaut. Highly insulting.

  • +132% growth from Q1 to peak 2024

  • +201% YoY growth

Supplements, nutraceuticals, and adaptogens are being flung across borders faster than conspiracy theories on TikTok. Why? Because unlike t-shirts, magnesium gummies don’t shrink, and they promise you’ll sleep like a Scandinavian lumberjack.

How does a Scandinavian Lumberjack sleep I hear you ask

Ah, the majestic Scandinavian slumberjack. Not to be confused with your average lumberjack , this one chops zzz’s, not trees. Here are three funny ways a Scandinavian slumberjack might catch some Nordic-style shuteye:

1. The Fjord Flop™
He cannonballs into bed like he's diving into a freezing fjord, then immediately enters a deep REM cycle wrapped in six ethically-sourced reindeer pelts. Occasionally murmurs “Uff da” in his sleep as a form of sleep-yodeling.

2. The IKEA Flatpack Nap
He dismantles himself into 14 labeled parts (legs, torso, beard, etc.) and reassembles into a fully horizontal sleeping position using only an Allen key and emotional resilience. Sleeps peacefully next to a scented candle called “Dozzklund.”

3. The Sauna Snooze Shuffle

He warms up in a log sauna at 110°C, then runs barefoot into the snow, does a snow angel, howls at the northern lights, and immediately collapses into a nap so intense it registers on the Richter scale. Wakes up mildly smoked and fully rested.

Check out my bedtime reading - “Nap Like a Norseman.”

Other verticals:

  • Beauty & Cosmetics: +92% to peak, but -14% under tariff weight.

  • Apparel: once glorious, now faltering with a YoY decline of -3%.

  • Consumer Goods: stable at 8% conversion, aka the "rice cake" of ecommerce.

Conversion = Trust x (Landed Costs – Sticker Shock)

Let’s talk conversion. You know, that sacred ecommerce KPI that turns browsers into buyers? It turns out that tariffs drop conversion by 30% when not pre-calculated. Surprise costs are the new villain origin story. Remember the kerfuffle when brands dared showed the tariffs in checkout, the cheek.

  • ANZ: 20% conversion (legendary)

  • North America: 18% (credit to Prime PTSD resilience)

  • LATAM: 5% (blame it on fees, corruption, and weather apps with better UX).

Geography of Spend: Average Order Value by Region

FlavorCloud's AOV breakdown reads like a socioeconomic Tinder profile:

  • Middle East: $160.86 - rich tastes, big baskets, perfume dreams.

  • Asia: $128.88 - high interest, lower retention.

  • Europe: $89.72 - tight wallets, stiff customs officers.

  • LATAM: $123.47 - potential if you can afford the bribes and bandwidth

Repeat Offenders: Where Loyalty Actually Exists

The holy grail of ecommerce isn’t acquisition, it’s retention. But it is largely a bolt on. The ones who do loyalty well have it in their DNA. They klnow it has to evolve and is more than a subscription model. Because your CAC ain’t paying for itself.

  • LATAM: 43% repeat purchase rate.

  • North America: 32% (grudging but faithful).

  • Asia: 21% (ghosted after one bad delivery experience).

But, like the mythical mountain Lion, is hiding in plain sight, to itself, but not anyone else. Finding them is quite the task. Loyalty though, is hard to earn. Anywhere. It is kept largely for the chosedn few.

B2B: The Forgotten Giant

Let’s be honest, most of the chatter is about DTC brands. But B2B is the $20.4 trillion elephant in the room—5x the size of B2C. Asia-Pacific owns 78% of it. Europe and the U.S.? Still asking their finance teams if they can invoice via PDF. And if you read my work at al, you will have read my papers on the investment of Private Equity into B2B commerce earlier this year. B2B involvement usually signals the beginning of the end though, right?

These guys are now borrowing DTC playbooks: air freight, automated customs clearance, and even SKU-level pricing. They’re doing Shopify, but on forklifts.

Tech-Enabled Trade: Buzzwords That Actually Work

Tech innovation investment has been enormous over the last decade. Trying to move the conversation beyond last mile cost and knowing their market has forced this part of supply chain into an uncomfortable area - post investment blues. Customer acquiring usually still starts at cost, capacity or missed opportunity. Then the tech can shine. But table stakes too, have changed. Let’s run through the greatest hits of modern logistics:

  • DDP (Delivered Duty Paid): No surprises = fewer cart abandonments.

  • 10-digit HS classification: Finally, AI used for something other than fake Drake tracks.

  • Localized Market Pricing: The psychological comfort of seeing your own currency + tax.

  • Dynamic Routing: Like Google Maps but for your serum.

  • Carrier Consolidation: DHL, FedEx, UPS—one day they’ll just form a band. DF*Ups I think it will be called. That’s for you Hendrik.

What Naomi Klein Would Say

If Naomi Klein were writing No Logo: The Cross-Border Edition, she’d rage against the myth of borderless consumer freedom. A t-shirt on your Instagram feed does not mean access. It means:

  • An import duty calculated by an algorithm in Toronto. Thanks Tobi.

  • A VAT pre-payment deducted by a Swedish fintech.Buy Now, Pay Never.

  • A customs declaration misfiled by a sleepy warehouse in Cleveland.RumpleStealthSkin.

What looked like liberation was actually fragmentation. The neoliberal fantasy of the frictionless market has become a Kafkaesque spreadsheet with drop-down menus for "country of origin" and "harmonized tariff subcode."

What’s Next: Cross Border 2030 (or The 7 Things That Will Definitely Happen Unless They Don’t)

  1. Tariffs Will Stay Petty – Global politics makes them worse, not better.

  2. AI Will Classify Your Socks – And it’ll be right 93% of the time.

  3. APAC & LATAM Will Own the Growth Narrative – Sorry, UK. You had a good run.

  4. Returns Will Become International Diplomacy – Reverse logistics meets NATO.

  5. B2B Brands Will Steal the DTC Playbook – And actually use it to scale.

  6. Localisation > Translation – Nobody trusts checkout that says "Ship via Planet Express or Buy With Prime for that matter."

  7. Your Grandma Will Subscribe to Chinese Probiotic Drops – Cross border is not just for Gen Z.

TL;DR: Borders Are the New Battle Lines of Ecommerce

Cross-border trade is the one-night stand that became a marriage of convenience. It’s messy, emotional, and involves too much paperwork. But with smart tools, decent strategy, and a brutal understanding of regional quirks, brands can survive—and thrive.

The winners? Brands that:

  • Show the true cost upfront.

  • Use tech like they mean it.

  • Know that a Brazilian shopper isn’t just an American with better taste in shoes.

And if that doesn’t work? Well... "this is my United States of Whatever."

Guitar riff out.

Commerce Platforms in European E-Commerce: Only the Beginning? Thanks to Kristian Mørk Puggaard CEO of Tembi - Market Intelligence for sharing this with our group this morning. His team build this useful data from Tembi’s analysis of commerce platforms across European e‑commerce markets. A few key stats stand out:

  • WooCommerce powers around 40% of stores across European markets, closely followed by Shopify at approximately 30%, together, they dominate with 70–73% of the market . Shopify grew their revenue in the EU in Q” 2029. It was at 49% growth after 8 quarters hovering around 33 - 35%. A little more effort and they got their just rewards.

  • In Denmark, WooCommerce accounts for about 15,447 webshops (39%), and Shopify follows at 14,689 (37%), together covering 76% of the market . Goog luck being Prestashop.

  • In Finland, WooCommerce holds around 44%, with Shopify at about 26%, totaling ~70%.

  • In countries like Slovakia, local platforms such as Shoptet outperform Shopify, thanks to better integration with regional marketplaces and services.

These numbers in isolation do not mean too much. It can help if you are a new platform (why bother) or to maybe help us understand why Scayle see North America as the place to grow or why Centra feel the EU is more ripe for their picking. It does help us to understand some of the dynamics though. The EU is more fragmented and despite not being sexy WooCommerce still holds a strong position of dominance. This data is not categorized, nor does it denote revenue but all shops are “live”. We do not see payment info or marketing technologies.

What would be interesting is to see the SI network, their partnerships and how that dynamic changes over the next 24 months. In north America this is not as much of a problem. It also suggests that true enterprise, as we think of it form a North American perspective has more depth in this space. It is not to say we do not have complicated, mature and technically proficient business requirements here. Quite the opposite when you factor in cross border trade and our continuing lack of unity despite our single currency area (joke.)

To build a more complete picture, here are some questions worth exploring:

What else should we consider to deepen the picture?

1. Market Coverage & Sample Size

  • Which countries are included in the analysis, and which are left out? I have mentioned some above.

  • How comprehensive is Tembi’s dataset? Does it capture both large and small operators? It seems to, but getting this breakout alone will help platforms and SIs work more effectively.

2. Platform Trends Over Time

  • How have market shares shifted over, say, the past 2–3 years? Is Shopify gaining faster than WooCommerce? Gaining is one thing. I would also posit that growth on platform is more interesting here and helps us consider:

  • Are there emerging challengers, global or local, that could disrupt the current balance? I mention Centra and Scayle - both gaining traction, both with ambitious goals.

3. Market Nuances by Country or Region

  • Platforms like Shoptet in Slovakia show the strength of local solutions. What other regional success stories exist? (E.g., MyCashFlow in Finland, Unas in Hungary, etc.) Partnerships matter, as does local knowledge.

  • What makes these local platforms successful, specific integrations, compliance, trusted reputation?

4. Platform Differentiators Beyond Architecture

  • Do merchants prefer WooCommerce for its open-source flexibility? Is Shopify favored for ease-of-use and SaaS reliability? Is Woo the long suffering incumbent.

  • What about platforms like PrestaShop, Shopware, are they significant contributors in certain markets? (E.g., PrestaShop in Lithuania or the Netherlands (Reddit), or Shopware's presence in Germany (Wikipedia))

5. Impact of Platform on Merchant Performance

  • Are Shopify merchants outperforming in site speed, UX, or conversion? They should be. If you are in the platform market, these are some of the areas foer consideration in your messaging.

  • Do WooCommerce shops have advantages in custom features like historical SEO or WordPress integration? How does this look into the future. Who is making the best partnerships when it comes to AI platforms.

6. Integration with Local Ecosystems

  • Platforms like Shoptet succeed by integrating with local marketplaces (e.g. Alza, Heureka). How well do platforms connect to essential services, payment methods, shipping providers, tax compliance?

7. Regulatory & Policy Context

  • How do EU regulations (e.g. DSA, geo‑blocking, VAT/IOSS rules) influence platform selection? Shopware has created competitive advantage in reg tech in the US using its EU framework. ICYMI.

  • Do some platforms better support compliance or even reduce merchant burden? See Shopware - again.

8. Broader Context: Marketplaces & Channels

  • Beyond standalone stores, vendors often sell via marketplaces. How do Amazon, eBay, Allegro, Zalando, Temu, etc., fit into this landscape? This is essential. Channel Engine, for example, have over 900 integrations. Approx 300 are in the EU.

  • Are commerce platforms simply one part of multichannel strategies that include social commerce, live shopping, TikTok Shop, and affiliate models now fueling purchase decisions? Is Shopify a platform anymore. That is a tongue in cheek joke before you pile on, Jeez.

9. Long-Term Outlook

  • Will the market consolidate further around two giants, or will AI-driven or omnichannel-native platforms emerge?

  • How will e-commerce evolution (e.g. social commerce, performance-based affiliate models) reshape platform needs and merchant preferences?

Tembi’s snapshot offers a strong foundation, but only the beginning. The real story lies in the trends, the local strategies, the merchant lifecycles, and the broader regulatory and marketplace ecosystems shaping platform choices.

Would love to hear from you:

  • What platform strategy are you seeing gain ground in your region?

  • Which platform trends or challenges should we monitor closely in 2026?

  • What questions would you add to deepen this picture even further?

  • What platforms should we cover for the Ostrich Report plat form?

In a world where technology meets tradition, comes a story of love, laughter, and logistics. The wait is over. The giant has arrived. Amazon, the overseas behemoth, is coming to a small town near you in Ireland.

The prequels have not all been pretty, but Amazon and Ireland could be a match made in heaven. Get ready for a romantic comedy like no other, with drama, twists, and turns that will make you laugh, cry, and turn heads.

Will this unlikely union bring prosperity or chaos? Find out in 2025, when Amazon comes to a small town near you in Ireland. Coming soon to theaters everywhere. Don't worry, you won’t miss it!"

The Back Story (Building characters and players up)

Amazon entering Ireland is like every other Amazon entry to a market and unlike it too. Ireland is a small, island economy. As a retail nation we have a few major points that Amazon can erode over time, little by little:

We have a large amount of retail resellers.

We have many chain stores who are struggling in home territories. They are in Ireland as part of a failed product/brand extension. ASk people who have tried this before. In our heads it makes sense, on the P and L, it does not. It never has.

According to best info, we have 217 retail parks in the country. If these were to be evenly distributed, this would be a park every 20km (rounded up). We have too many .

We have approx 24,500 retail stores in 2021. Categorised as follows:

Convenience stores and grocery make up 50% of our retail footprint. This is not the initial target but strategic acquisitions would make it interesting.

During COVID, we all proved we could build a Shopify store and run ads. Now the wheels have come off for many. There are plenty of influencer led brands emerged but as in other countries, do they have a life span. My view is influencer/celebrity brands should be run to sell trend based products, not to fill a category and hope you can expand outwards. We simply do not have the market to do it. When we go over the pond, we get overwhelmed. Let’s not forget Greater Manchester is bigger than Ireland. In the US, there are 143 “Ireland’s “ or cities with < than 6M people. That is a lot of demographic change, behavioural nuance and learning.

As I said, Ireland needed a Co-oP. It has landed. But I think it is worth breaking it down to see what this means for people. But a few key topics emerged for me and through the magic of cinema, I am going to bring them to life. Call this Episode 1.

The Curse of Prime Delivery - It’s Fast and we’re Furious.

In the high-octane world of retail, Amazon has been the undisputed champion of fast and free delivery, leaving competitors in the dust. Let's compare Amazon's impact on next-day and free delivery in the UK over the years, how retailers have responded, and the pressures it has imposed on decision-making.

Amazon's Turbocharged Delivery

  • Next-Day Delivery: Amazon's Prime service has revolutionized the delivery landscape with its next-day and same-day options. By 2024, Amazon delivered over a billion items in the UK within a day or the next, setting a new benchmark for speed1. This has forced competitors to rev up their engines, offering similar services to keep pace. In the US 200 prime members enjoyed the delivery of over 9BN parcels in 2024 or 1 per week. Prime and its penetration will be a key watching metric for those looking to impacts.

  • Free Delivery: Initially, Amazon offered free delivery on orders over £25. However, in a recent move, the threshold was increased to £35, pushing non-Prime customers to either spend more or face delivery charges2. This strategic shift aims to encourage more customers to join Prime, further solidifying Amazon's grip on the market. This is going to impact retailers around the country and opens up more discussion on buy online, pick up in store.

Retailers' Response: The Need for Speed

Retailers have responded by adopting faster delivery options, but many struggle to match Amazon's scale and efficiency. The pressure to offer next-day delivery has become a significant challenge, with missed deliveries costing UK businesses £1.6 billion annually6. To stay competitive, retailers feel they must invest in smarter logistics and warehouse operations, often at the cost of profitability.But do they need this? Is the smart move now FBA?.

Pressures on Decision-Making: The High-Stakes Game

Amazon's dominance has imposed immense pressure on retailers to adapt quickly. The dynamic pricing model and fast delivery expectations have forced competitors to be agile and responsive. However, this race for speed and price competitiveness can be a double-edged sword. While it drives innovation, it also risks undermining profitability and sustainability for smaller retailers.

The Obsession: A Noose for Others?

Amazon's relentless pursuit of speed and efficiency has become a benchmark that others struggle to meet. This obsession with fast and free delivery has created a high-stakes environment where smaller retailers may find it difficult to survive. The increased costs of maintaining such services, combined with the need to match Amazon's pricing strategies, can be overwhelming. In this "Fast and Furious" world of retail, you have to decide if you are Paul Walker or Vin Diesel.

"Retailball: The Art of Winning in a Changing Game"

In a world where the retail landscape is as unpredictable as a baseball season, one man, Jack Harris, stood at the helm of a struggling retail chain. Jack was the Billy Beane of retail, determined to challenge traditional methods and find a winning strategy amidst the chaos. His team, like the Oakland A's, was underdogged by the giants of e-commerce, particularly Amazon, with its unparalleled mindshare and distribution capabilities.

The Challenge: Amazon's Dominance

Amazon's influence on the retail industry was akin to a home run in the bottom of the ninth inning—it changed the game entirely. With its vast distribution network and innovative fulfillment strategies, Amazon had set a new standard for customer expectations. Traditional retailers, like Jack's chain, were left scrambling to keep up. The high operating costs, complex supply chain management, and the need for digital transformation made it difficult for brick-and-mortar stores to compete34.

The Opportunity Costs

Jack faced a dilemma similar to Billy Beane's in "Moneyball." He had to decide whether to invest in more physical stores or pivot towards a more digital strategy. Each choice came with significant opportunity costs. Expanding physical presence meant higher overheads and less flexibility, while going digital required a complete overhaul of their business model. Jack realized that the traditional retail model was no longer viable; it was time to rethink distribution and focus on profitability rather than sheer store count. This is the conversation going on in stores all around the country now. 90% of those present at the partner day last week said, they were not even after taking the first steps. There is my worry.

The Sunk Costs

Many retailers were clinging to their existing strategies, much like Beane's reluctance to let go of underperforming players. Jack understood that past investments couldn't dictate future decisions. He needed to cut losses and adapt to the changing retail landscape. This meant embracing Amazon's strengths, not fighting them. Jack considered partnering with Amazon or leveraging its advertising platform to reach a broader audience.

The Comparative Advantage

Just as the Oakland A's leveraged players' unique skills, Jack sought to identify his chain's comparative advantages. They excelled in providing personalized customer experiences and curated product selections, something Amazon couldn't replicate. By focusing on these strengths, Jack aimed to carve out a niche in the market where his stores could thrive alongside, rather than against, Amazon's dominance. It is not necessarily how you have done business to date, it’s how you expand on how did things, being key.

The Statistical Discrimination

In "Moneyball," statistical analysis revolutionized player selection. Jack applied a similar approach to his retail strategy. He used data analytics to understand consumer behavior, optimize inventory, and tailor marketing efforts. This data-driven approach allowed him to make informed decisions about store locations and product offerings, ensuring each store was a home run in its market.

The Principle-Agent Problem - The Night Agent

Jack faced the challenge of aligning his team's goals with the company's overall strategy. He needed to motivate his staff to embrace change and work towards a more efficient, digitally integrated model. By empowering them with the tools and training necessary for success, Jack ensured that everyone was working towards the same objective: winning in the new retail game.

As Jack navigated the complex world of retail, he realized that success wasn't about beating Amazon but about finding a way to coexist and thrive. By leveraging Amazon's strengths while focusing on his own comparative advantages, Jack created a winning strategy. "Retailball" became a story of innovation over tradition, where the underdog retailer found a way to stay in the game by embracing change and optimizing for profitability in a rapidly evolving retail landscape.

Jack Harris and his team embody the spirit of "Moneyball," using strategic decision-making and resource allocation to navigate the challenges posed by Amazon's dominance. By focusing on their unique strengths and adapting to the changing retail landscape, they find a path to success in a market where traditional models are no longer viable.

Rightsizing Retail Stores

On Saturday last, I spoke with Bobby Kerr (Thanks @john fardy). The role of down sizinig or exiting a market is not truly rtold through occupancy figures. Jervis Streeet shopping centre is to be sold for 50% of its highest valuation despite, occupancy not being a probelm at all. Over 35% of the retail outlets are food chains. Jervis itself is in close proxiomity to Arnotts and other affordable stores. It is also a terrible looking building. There is no "Gra" in this place whatsoever. Experiential, it aint.

The reality is that the retail industry is undergoing a significant transformation, with many brands reassessing their store counts due to over-supply and distribution challenges. This trend is evident in the rapid pace of store closures across the U.S., with about 15,000 retail stores expected to close in 2025, significantly higher than the 7,325 closures in 2024. This shift reflects a broader strategy to optimize retail operations, focusing on profitability and efficiency rather than extensive physical presence.

Key Factors Influencing Store Closures

  1. E-commerce Growth: The convenience and competitive pricing of online shopping have led consumers to shift away from traditional brick-and-mortar stores.

  2. Economic Pressures: Inflation, supply chain disruptions, and changing consumer spending habits have strained retailers’ profitability.

  3. Overexpansion: Some retailers expanded rapidly without sustainable demand, leading to financial overreach.

Sustainability and Consumerism

Using sustainability as a lens, it's clear that consumers are increasingly questioning whether they have too much stuff. The fast fashion industry, in particular, is under scrutiny due to its environmental impact and unsustainable practices. Fast fashion encourages overconsumption, leading to massive textile waste—Americans generate about 82 pounds of textile waste annually. This has prompted consumers to favor brands that prioritize sustainability, with 70% willing to pay more for sustainable products.

Fast Fashion at Risk

Fast fashion brands are facing significant challenges due to their unsustainable practices and the growing demand for eco-friendly products. Brands like Quiz, a UK-based clothing retailer, have struggled in recent years.

Quiz clothing once posed a model for balance and growth. And Allbirds SEC S-1 Filing presented a case for utopian commerce. Both are now floundering with Quiz in adminstration and Allbirds in a turnaround strategy. Pray for Allbirds.

Quiz: A Timeline of Challenges

  • 2020: Quiz underwent a restructuring, renegotiating rents after lockdowns damaged sales. At this time, they adopted a healthy approach to convessions and internationalization.

  • 2023-2024: Quiz faced declining sales, with UK online operations severely impacted by economic pressures. Despite a 12% increase in international demand, overall sales declined.

  • December 2024: Quiz warned of running out of cash by early 2025, seeking additional funding due to a significant reduction in revenue.

  • February 2025: Quiz fell into administration, with Teneo handling the process. This led to the closure of 23 shops and about 200 redundancies.

Allbirds: A Sustainable Model Under Pressure

Allbirds, known for its sustainable footwear, initially thrived with a strong brand identity and commitment to eco-friendly practices. However, the brand has recently faced declining sales and store closures due to supply chain disruptions and shifting consumer behaviors. When they filed they S-1, pre IPO, they had a Utopian looking business model.

Their wrong decisions, now a glorious cautionary tale - stay in your lane.

Our growth will largely depend on our ability to successfully open and operate new stores, which depends on many factors, including, among others, our ability to:

•identify suitable store locations, the availability of which is outside of our control and may require expensive and long-term lease obligations;

•gain brand recognition and acceptance, particularly in geographies or regions that are new to us;

•negotiate acceptable lease terms;

•hire, train, and retain store personnel and field management who possess the required customer service and other skills and who share our commitment to sustainability;

•invest sufficient capital in store build-out and opening;

•immerse new store personnel and field management into our corporate culture and shared values;

•source sufficient inventory levels; and

•successfully integrate new stores into our existing operations and information technology systems.

Allbirds: Key Decision Points

  • 2020: Allbirds reported revenue of $219 million, up 13.2% from the previous year.

  • 2021: Revenue increased to $277 million, a 26.5% rise.

  • 2022: Revenue reached $298 million, up 7.3%.

  • 2023: Revenue declined to $254 million, a 14% drop.

  • 2024: Forecasted revenue was $191 million, a 25% decrease from 2023.

  • 2024: Allbirds announced plans to close 10-15 underperforming U.S. stores, focusing on optimizing its store footprint and product offerings.

Ecommerce Strategies for Growth

Ecommerce plays a crucial role in retail growth, especially in expanding customer bases and international reach. Retailers must navigate challenges such as subpar on-site search functionality and adapt to shifting consumer behaviors. Successful ecommerce strategies often involve AI-driven personalization, mobile optimization, and omnichannel experiences.

It is not the be all and end all. Customer trends move quick, very quick. The idea of long term brands is a tough consideration.

Key Ecommerce Trends for 2025

  1. Marketplaces: Marketplaces continue to drive consistent growth, offering expanded product offerings, reduced operational costs, and improved customer experiences.

  2. Retail Media: Retail media strategies are becoming essential for targeted advertising and customer engagement

  3. AI Integration: AI is increasingly a core strategic pillar for enhancing customer experiences and operational efficiency.

Sustainable Ecommerce Practices

As consumers become more environmentally conscious, sustainable ecommerce practices are gaining traction. These include eco-friendly packaging innovations, green supply chain management, and energy-efficient data centers. Retailers can leverage these practices to reduce environmental impact, boost brand loyalty, and potentially increase profits.

As I come back to reality, I am thinking.

  1. Rightsizing Retail Stores: How can retailers balance physical presence with ecommerce strategies to optimize profitability?

  2. Sustainability and Consumerism: What role do consumers play in driving demand for sustainable products, and how can retailers respond effectively?Does it matter anymore? Is sustainability the new DEI.

  3. Fast Fashion at Risk: How can fast fashion brands transition towards more sustainable practices without sacrificing profitability? OR should fast fashion exist at all, is there a new way to deliver this.

  4. Ecommerce Strategies: What are the most effective ecommerce strategies for expanding customer bases and international reach in the retail sector? Internationalisation is one of the last growth pillars, where does it sit in the mix?

Welcome to another episode of Billions, but not the one you're used to. Today, we're not stalking the halls of Wall Street or scheming in smoke-glassed boardrooms. We’re heading to the frontline of another high-stakes arena: UK retail.

The battleground is data.

The players? Brands, buyers, bots, and billions on the line.

But your guides? Bobby Axelrod, the billionaire with a sixth sense for blood in the water, and Chuck Rhoades, the state’s attorney turned ethics crusader. Together, they’ll pull apart the 2025 UK Retail Index like it’s a deposition transcript with something to hide.

CHAPTER ONE: GEN Z SCROLLS, BOOMERS STROLL

Chuck:
“We are not rational actors, Bobby. We think we’re choosing based on values, but what we’re really doing is seeking validation. And validation, in retail, means dopamine and delivery windows.”

The report claims that 41% of Gen Z are buying directly from social media. It paints a world where TikTok is the new town square, and Instagram is a department store. But let’s be honest—scrolling and buying are not the same. Conversion rates on social platforms? Still wildly inefficient.

Axe:
“Chuck, here’s the thing. Everyone’s treating Gen Z like they’re some unknowable alien species. They want what everyone wants—convenience, clout, and a reason to spend mum’s money. If 53% of shoppers will abandon a purchase over bad payment UX, then forget TikTok filters. Give them Klarna and a one-click checkout.”

What the Index doesn't say? The average cart abandonment rate across all channels is still north of 70%. We’re talking ghost towns in digital storefronts.

CHAPTER TWO: AI—THE BIG BLUFF?

Me: AI. The future we were promised. The future we now mistrust. According to the report, half of consumers don’t like interacting with AI. Yet 66% understand its role in making product suggestions. This is not a love story. It's a marriage of convenience with a pre-nup , the “opt-out.”

Chuck:
“I’ve spent my career identifying what people say they want versus what they do. AI in retail is the ultimate surveillance capitalism riddle. Do we want magic or privacy? You don’t get both.”

Axe:
“Consumers say they hate AI? Yeah, until it nails their size, gets the right brand, and sends them 20% off. You think ChatGPT shopping is fringe? It’s already mainstream. 35% of consumers have used AI assistants while shopping. The other 65% are lying or just slow.”

The contrarian stat? AI usage in sales and marketing is only at 26% investment by retailers. That’s not a surge; that’s hesitation. Everyone’s waiting for someone else to screw it up first.

CHAPTER THREE: BRICK & MORTAR—ZOMBIE OR ZEN?

The Index gushes over in-store appeal. 52% of store loyalists love to touch and feel products. 30% still say it’s their preferred channel. A quaint notion, almost nostalgic. But nostalgia doesn’t move inventory.

Axe:
“In-store isn’t dead. It’s just drunk and disoriented. Retailers are investing in experiential shopping? Translation: they’re putting neon signs on a sinking ship.”

Chuck:
“I disagree. The physical store is our last bastion of restraint. No infinite scroll, no algorithmic nudges. Just shelves and consequences.”

Only 29% of retailers are actually investing in tech to improve the in-store experience. And while the Index praises POS innovation, most brands are still fumbling with ancient terminals and staff that can’t split a bill—never mind upsell with AI support.

CHAPTER FOUR: PERSONALISATION—INTIMATE OR INVASIVE?

Me: Welcome to the personalization paradox.

36% of consumers expect tailored experiences. 62% prefer brands offering discounts via loyalty programs. Yet there's a rising unease—a sense that personalization is a fancy word for surveillance.

Chuck:
“This is where capitalism eats its own tail. We offer ‘tailored experiences,’ and in return, we harvest behaviors. Then we feign surprise when trust collapses.”

Axe:
“You call it surveillance. I call it sales. If loyalty schemes aren’t delivering, it’s not because people hate them—it’s because they’re boring. If your points system feels like collecting stamps at a diner, then yeah, it fails.”

The external reality? McKinsey data shows personalization can deliver a 10-15% revenue lift, but only when executed across all customer touchpoints. Without connected data, it's lipstick on a dashboard. Omni versus Multi in a nutshell.

CHAPTER FIVE: PAYMENT COSTS—THE INVISIBLE BATTLEFIELD

Me: Beneath every checkout flow lies a warzone. Fraud, fees, reconciliation nightmares. The Index reveals that 32% of businesses believe offering local payment methods can reduce fees. But only 22% are proactively targeting payment cost reductions as a lever to grow revenue.

Axe:
“That’s rookie math. You don’t grow by slashing—unless you’re cutting dead weight. If your payment provider’s choking your margin, fire them.”

Chuck:
“What’s astonishing isn’t the fraud. It’s the lack of systems to prevent it. 29% say fraud attempts increased, but no one’s talking about layered authentication or behavioural biometrics.”

And let’s not ignore the irony. Brands will obsess over bounce rates and CPMs, but can’t even tell you their net effective transaction cost after returns and fraud.

CHAPTER SIX: PAYMENTS—FAST, FLAWLESS OR FORGOTTEN?

86% of businesses without high-reliability payment systems report revenue loss due to downtime. 52% of shoppers say checkout delays lead to abandonment. And yet, half the brands you interact with still treat payment as plumbing.

Chuck :
“I’ve prosecuted cybercrime rings with better operational redundancy than some payment stacks.”

Axe:
“This is where real money gets made—or lost. Unified commerce? That’s not just jargon. That’s a 15% lift in AOV for those who get it right.”

If you’re not investing in low-latency, multi-rail payment infrastructure in 2025, you might as well close early and turn off the lights.

CHAPTER SEVEN: EXPANSION—MARKETPLACE MADNESS

30% of businesses plan to become marketplaces. A tempting model. Low inventory. High margin. Global scale. But there’s a catch.

Axe:
“Everyone wants to be Amazon until they hit VAT compliance in 12 countries and a wave of counterfeit returns.”

Chuck:
“You don’t get to scale without structure. Marketplaces work when trust and logistics are industrial-grade. Otherwise, you’re just a chaotic swap meet with a URL.”

23% also plan international expansion. But with Brexit baggage and geopolitical friction, expanding outside the UK isn’t just a growth lever—it’s a gamble.

CHAPTER EIGHT: ETHICS—THE PERFORMANCE OF PURPOSE

79% of consumers say they donate to charity. 44% say they’d be more loyal to retailers who contribute to causes. A PwC survey claims consumers will even pay a 9.7% “sustainability premium.” But only 29% of retailers offer donation options online.

Chuck:
“Consumers aren’t just wallets. They’re citizens. Retailers who ignore that are writing their own obituaries.”

Axe:*leaves the room for this one*

Retail’s sustainability rhetoric is often a veneer. Brands still pump out fast fashion, ship single items in three boxes, and call it “eco-conscious” because the box has a green leaf on it.

beneath the glossy graphs is a sector at war with itself. Innovation battling inertia. Data mining posing as personalization. And ethical claims clashing with cold margins.

Taken from the Adyen UK Index 2025
