On this day in 1989 a seismic shift in culture and entertainment occurred, the Simpsons was born. The episode was titled Simpsons roasting on an open Fire and thankfully it was a Christmas episode. Now, purists will tell me about Tracy Ullman show, but this was the full episodic length show. 30 minutes long. Here we are 36 years later looking to Homer and the family for inspiration, direction and for a laugh.

The Simpsons has functioned as a funhouse mirror for modern life: exaggerating our politics, families, and institutions just enough that their absurdity snaps into focus, while accidentally feeling more prophetic the longer it runs. Sadly and ironically at times. It helped invent a smarter, more cynical, more reference‑dense style of comedy that now underpins everything from Family Guy to contemporary prestige sitcoms.​ In case you didn’t notice, I reference it, ALOT.

Holding a mirror to us

From the start, Springfield was built as a microcosm of America: a town where environmental disasters, corrupt politicians, corporate greed, media sensationalism, and religious hypocrisy all sit a block apart from a fairly ordinary family. Episodes routinely tackled topics like pollution (“Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish”), consumerism (“Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy”), immigration (“Much Apu About Nothing”), and gay rights (“Homer’s Phobia”) long before they were default TV fare.​

The show’s genius is that kids could laugh at slapstick while adults caught the jokes about Fox News, culture wars, and failing public institutions, training viewers to see politics and media with a skeptical eye. That tone helped normalize a more openly cynical, “of course the system is rigged” attitude that now feels baked into online culture and late‑night comedy.​

The “predictions” phenomenon

The “Simpsons predicted it” meme works because the show has produced thousands of hyper‑specific gags about tech, politics, and culture over three decades; enough darts and some will hit the board. But some episodes are strikingly on‑the‑nose:​

  • “Bart to the Future” (Season 11, 2000) casually mentions Donald Trump as a former U.S. president, years before his real‑world election.​

  • “Lisa’s Wedding” (Season 6) imagines video calling on a hybrid phone‑screen device that looks uncannily like modern FaceTime.​

  • “Lisa the Greek” (Season 3) correctly tracks multiple Super Bowl winners via re‑dubbed dialogue over several years, turning a character bit into a minor sports‑prediction legend.​

  • “Marge in Chains” (Season 4) shows a flu‑like virus, panic buying, and an angry mob breaking open a crate of “killer bees,” later read as echoing Covid‑era shortages and murder‑hornet headlines.​

  • Many more have followed since, but when you think of the job of the writers - “think of the most absurd outcome for this possibility”, this is where we end up.

And what looks like clairvoyance is mostly sharp satire plus a huge sample size, but it also underscores how often the show anticipated the logical endpoint of trends in politics, media, and technology.​

It’s writers were not your average Motley crew.

  • Al Jean: Graduated from Harvard University with a bachelor’s degree in mathematics at age 16 and served as executive producer and head writer.

  • David S. Cohen (David X. Cohen): Earned a bachelor’s degree in physics from Harvard University and a master’s in computer science from UC Berkeley; he later co-created Futurama with Matt Groening.

  • Ken Keeler: Holds a bachelor’s and a PhD in applied mathematics from Harvard University, as well as a master’s in electrical engineering from Stanford.

  • Jeff Westbrook: Resigned from a senior research post as an associate professor at Yale University to write for the show. He has a PhD in computer science from Princeton University.

  • Bill Odenkirk: Earned a PhD in inorganic chemistry from the University of Chicago.

  • Matt Groening: The show’s creator, attended The Evergreen State College, where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in journalism and was the editor of the school newspaper.

  • Conan O’Brien: The former late-night host and a former writer for the show, graduated magna cum laude from Harvard University with a degree in history and literature

Its place in society

By the late 1990s, The Simpsons had gone from “bad role model” (banned T‑shirts, George H. W. Bush’s jab that families should be “more like the Waltons and less like the Simpsons”) to canonical Americana. It reshaped TV comedy with dense pop‑culture references, rapid‑fire gags, and emotional beats that treated animated characters as fully human, a template that shows like Futurama, South Park, and BoJack Horseman build on.​

It also rewired everyday language: “D’oh!” entered dictionaries, and words like “cromulent” and “embiggen” escaped into real‑world usage, evidence of how deeply the show invaded the vernacular. After 30‑plus seasons, The Simpsons functions almost like a cultural operating system: a shared reference set people use to talk about politics, work, family, and the feeling that everything is a bit rigged and ridiculous.​

Black Mirror Time - Simpsons Quotes: where we are as a society

Below are quotes that double as social barometer, lines you can almost drop straight onto a Twitter/X feed or a political stump speech and they still land.

Homer Simpson

  • “Just because I don’t care doesn’t mean I don’t understand.”​

  • “I’m not a bad guy! I work hard, and I love my kids. So why should I spend half my Sunday hearing about how I’m going to hell?”​

  • “Alcohol: the cause of, and solution to, all of life’s problems.”​

  • “If something’s hard to do, then it’s not worth doing.”​

  • “Trying is the first step toward failure.”​

Mayor Quimby

  • “I stand by my racial slur.”​

  • “I’d like to remind everyone that I was elected by the narrowest of margins, and I can be replaced just as easily.”​

  • “I propose that I use what’s left of the town treasury to move to a more prosperous town and run for mayor there. Once elected, I will send for the rest of you.”​

  • “This time he’s the lesser of two evils.” (Campaign slogan.)​

Moe Szyslak

  • “I’m better than dirt. Well, most kinds of dirt. Not that fancy store‑bought dirt. That stuff’s loaded with nutrients. I can’t compete with that.”​

  • “Oh, loneliness and cheeseburgers are a dangerous mix.”​

  • “I’ve done things I’m not proud of, and the things I am proud of are disgusting.”​

  • “Good God! Homer, you know I support most any prejudice you can name, but your hero‑phobia sickens me.”​

Taken together, those quotes and episodes sketch out the show’s core thesis: we are ridiculous, frequently venal, often lazy or corrupt, but also recognizably human and the systems around us are only as absurd as we let them be.

The Simpsons, to me is one of those moments of where a notable shift occurred. Today, Dec 17th 2025, we are in the midst of many more, one most notable being AI. Sadly, it is the misuse of the technology that is becoming the palace that energy goes and for all the wrong reasons. Imagine we realised the technology capabilities as a society and moved to harvest it for good. I am sure, at some point we will do this though. Right?

In ecommerce our job now is to live amidst all of this and make sense of it all in ways that are useful to our lifestyle and that pave the path to glory. Or at least for now survival. 2025 provided some things to note that are more shift that trend to me.

The Seven Allocation Shocks: How 2025 Rewired Where Ecommerce GMV Actually Went

There is a difference between a trend and a shift. I spoke about this before. In Sean Dowling’s economics class in September of 198, I was first introduced to the topic.

A shift in economics refers to a change in an entire curve (such as supply or demand) caused by an external factor other than the price of the good itself, leading to a new equilibrium. A trend, on the other hand, describes a long-term, underlying direction or general movement in economic data, such as a steady increase in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over a period of many years, often reflecting fundamental changes in the economy.

This year we experienced both, all at the same time. This, I realised, is the job. Operating on both of these curves, always and forever.

If you only looked at topline ecommerce numbers in 2025, you could convince yourself not much changed.
Growth was… fine. Nothing like the 2020‑2021 sugar high, but not a catastrophe either. A sort of stubborn, grinding normality. Thank you discounting and BNPL (who we will hear from later).

But spend five minutes inside a P&L or a data warehouse and it’s obvious something else was going on.
GMV didn’t just “grow”. It rerouted. It slipped out of some hands and into others, often without anyone really noticing until the quarter was over and someone in finance started asking awkward questions.

What follows is my tour through the seven big stories that actually shaped where the money went this year:

  1. Agentic AI stopped being a slide and started quietly routing demand.

  2. Tariffs and the death of de minimis broke the ultra‑cheap China model.

  3. Marketplaces pivoted into “local” to survive that shock.

  4. BNPL’s regulatory hangover changed how carts were financed.

  5. Retail media turned shelf space into an auction.

  6. Cross‑border got risk‑priced; inventory got closer to home.

  7. AI‑powered owned sites tried to fight back against marketplace gravity.

If you’re a brand, retailer, or marketplace operator, the question is no longer “is ecommerce growing?” but “who is the new traffic cop, and what are they optimizing for?”

Let’s get into it.

Agentic AI: When the Shopper Isn’t Really the Shopper Anymore

Somewhere around mid‑2025, shopping agents stopped being a demo and started showing up in real traffic logs. Not as a big bang, not as “everyone now uses an AI concierge,” but as a steady rise of odd‑looking sessions: cleaner referral headers, fewer page views per session, higher intent, faster checkouts.

What changed? Three things.

  • Browsers and super‑apps quietly rolled out “do my shopping” flows: you tell the agent the brief and budget, and it brings back a shortlist, often with one‑click checkout.

  • The big consulting/strategy decks stopped calling this “a future scenario” and started treating agentic commerce as an actual, near‑term channel that brands needed to design for.

  • Consumers, tired, time‑poor, and already delegating decisions to algorithms in other parts of life, didn’t really resist. They just slid into it the way they slid into one‑click checkouts and saved cards.

The number that matters here isn’t adoption in some abstract “% of shoppers using AI” sense.
It’s the share of GMV that passes through an algorithmic intermediary that can compare you to everyone else in milliseconds and has no emotional attachment to your brand.

How that moved GMV

Agentic AI did two big things to GMV allocation this year:

  • It punished anyone whose catalog and data were a mess.
    Agents don’t care about your brand story if they can’t read your size curves, ingredients, compatibility, shipping rules, or live price in a structured way. Retailers and brands with rich, standardized feeds and clean product data were picked more often because agents could actually evaluate them.

  • It rewarded whoever was set up to “win the query,” not “own the customer.”
    If the agent’s job is to minimize hassle, maximize value, and reduce risk for the shopper, then GMV shifted toward players who were competitive on price, shipping, and availability in real time. That often meant big marketplaces, large multi‑brand retailers, and a handful of high‑signal DTCs with strong ratings and low friction.

Your old funnel thinking awareness, consideration, conversion doesn’t map neatly to a world where an AI agent compresses half your funnel into a single step. Why I feel this is noteworthy, all BFCM reports include their AI “take” - where ecommerce once resided, AI and agentic are now the residents.

How brands reacted

As you thought you should, move early gain an advantage - Arbitrage. The smart ones stopped treating this as “SEO, but with more buzzwords” and started doing three unglamorous things:

  • Fixing the pipes: product attributes, taxonomy, structured content, live pricing and availability feeds got board‑level attention. Not because it looks nice in the UX, but because agents literally won’t pick you if you don’t show up clean and comparable.

  • Negotiating with the new gatekeepers: from search engines to marketplaces to retail media networks, brands started asking “how does your agent rank options, and what do I have to do to be in the top three?”

  • Experimenting with “agent‑specific” offers: better bundles, dynamic discounts, or warranties surfaced only to certain intermediaries, to see how the ranking logic responded.

A few brands made the opposite call: opt out as much as possible, double down on first‑party relationships, and lean into categories where human preference and identity still dominate (fashion, beauty, hobbies). These behaviors are in direct contrast to brands being asked to fix data or develop SEO strategies instead of relying on paid media. Hmmm.

How consumers responded

Most people didn’t sit around saying, “today I will embrace agentic commerce.”
They just started using the AI button when it made their life easier.

The pattern:

  • Agents for the boring stuff: replenishment, basic home goods, “I just need a decent cable that arrives tomorrow.”

  • Humans for the identity stuff: “I want a jacket that feels like me,” “I care about this brand’s ethics,” “I don’t trust a bot to choose my skincare.”

GMV followed that line: high‑frequency, low‑emotion spend quietly migrated toward whoever played best with the agents. The rest stayed messy, human, and up for grabs.

Tariffs, De Minimis, and the Great Cheap China Reset

In April and May, the other big story hit: the United States finally went after the tidal wave of cheap parcels coming in under the de minimis threshold. The Trump administration tore up the “sub‑$800 gets in duty‑free” rule and layered new tariffs on top, with some categories facing triple‑digit effective rates.

Temu, Shein, and the entire class of ultra‑low‑cost exporters were the obvious primary targets.
For a while, they’d effectively been riding a structural arbitrage: rock‑bottom manufacturing costs, direct entry into the U.S. postal stream, and no duties.

That model had limits, and 2025 found them.

How that moved GMV

Once tariffs and the end of de minimis started to bite, three things happened quickly:

  • Prices on the apps went up.
    Headlines about “import charges,” “extra fees at checkout,” and “your order may incur additional costs” did exactly what you’d expect to conversion rates.​

  • Marketing budgets pulled back.
    When every parcel costs more to get into the U.S., the ROI on blasting performance ads at marginal customers falls. Chinese cross‑border players shifted spend away from hyper‑aggressive U.S. acquisition and toward Europe and other markets with looser rules.

  • GMV leaked back into domestic value formats.
    Once the price delta between a Temu basic and a Walmart/Amazon private‑label basic narrowed, the “I’ll wait three weeks for it to arrive from who‑knows‑where” proposition made less sense for a meaningful chunk of shoppers. GMV drifted back to dollar stores, off‑price chains, and mainstream marketplaces where the trade‑off between price, trust, and speed looked better.

How brands and marketplaces responded

If you were a U.S. value retailer, this was a gift.
Suddenly, “cheap but slow” had to fight harder against “cheap enough and here tomorrow.”

  • U.S. retailers leaned harder into private label and “good enough” ranges, tightening value messaging and inventory depth in basic categories hit hardest by Chinese competition.

  • Amazon and large marketplaces quietly widened their own price ladders, you could still find the ultra‑cheap stuff, but there was more emphasis on reasonably priced, Prime‑eligible lternatives.

On the other side of the Pacific, Chinese platforms moved fast:

  • More local warehousing, more U.S. 3PL partnerships, more SKUs pre‑cleared through customs.

  • A stronger push into “local seller” models where the inventory never crosses a border at all, just the customer relationship. (We’ll come back to that with Temu’s local seller play.

Make no bones about it either, the Chinese platforms have anticipated these moves and already stepped beyond these boundaries. Their models evolved and are now quietly back in the driving seat.

How consumers responded

The user behavior shift was subtle but important:

  • Heavy Temu/Shein users didn’t abandon them overnight, but they cut back the frivolous, experimental baskets, the fifth novelty kitchen gadget, the “it’s only $3” impulse buys.

  • More of those low‑stakes purchases went back to Amazon, Walmart, and local discounters, where the price gap was smaller but the trust and delivery speed were higher.

The “ultra‑cheap everything” era didn’t end, but the free lunch got a lot more expensive. GMV rebalanced accordingly.

Temu, Local Sellers, and the Marketplace Pivot to “Here, Not There”

Chinese platforms do not f*ck about. Faced with tariffs and political pressure, Temu did something strategically smart: it stopped betting everything on cross‑border arbitrage and started acting more like a conventional marketplace in some markets.

The Local Seller Program, launched late 2024 and scaled in 2025, opened the doors to businesses outside China who could list on Temu and fulfill locally
The Shopify app that dropped this week is the most visible version of that: millions of Shopify merchants can now pipe their catalog into Temu, manage inventory and orders from one place, and reach Temu’s audience without shipping from Shenzhen.

How that moved GMV

This did two interesting things to GMV allocation:

  • It changed what GMV Temu was capturing.
    Instead of 100% cross‑border cheap stuff, Temu’s mix tilted toward local inventory in 30+ markets, including the U.S., Canada, UK, Germany, Spain, and Australia. That means some GMV that might have happened on a brand’s own Shopify storefront, or on another marketplace, is now happening inside Temu’s app, but fulfilled from a warehouse down the road.

  • It softened the tariff blow without fully escaping it.
    Local inventory isn’t tariff‑free forever (somebody still imported those goods), but once it’s in‑market and duties are paid, you can ship domestically at predictable cost. GMV gets re‑routed from “many parcels crossing customs individually” to “bulk shipments + local last mile.”

Underneath the political noise, this is just marketplaces evolving to match the new risk/reward equation of Cross‑border.Marketplaces, experience a quiet resurgence.

How brands responded

For Shopify merchants and SMB brands, Temu’s local seller rails look like any other incremental channel:

  • A place to chase new demand with relatively low integration friction.

  • A way to move surplus inventory or test price points without fully re‑architecting their own site.

    That said, the more sophisticated brands immediately recognized the familiar Amazon problem:

  • Channel strategy suddenly matters again. If your SKUs are on Amazon, TikTok Shop, Temu, and your own site, the risk of price compression, gray‑market resellers, and brand dilution rises fast. Larger brands moved to stricter assortment segmentation, MAP enforcement, and packaging variants to keep some control over where GMV shows up and at what price.

How consumers responded

From the shopper’s perspective, Temu started to feel a bit different:

  • More recognizable brands in the feed.

  • Slightly faster and more reliable deliveries on some items.

    More “this shipped from your country” messaging to rebuild trust.

That combination nudged some spend that might have gone to Amazon, Etsy, or even independent sites into the Temu ecosystem instead. The marketplace playbook repeats, just with a new cast. Since I started writing this Shopify have announced that the Temu native app exists now in their Shopify store, just like Klaviyo and eBay.

BNPL’s Regulatory Hangover and the Quiet Checkout Re‑Rank

While everyone was watching tariffs and AI, regulators were finally catching up with Buy Now, Pay Later. In the UK and Europe especially, 2025 was the year BNPL went from “light‑touch” to “you are now very much regulated credit.”

Consultations, draft rules, and implementation timelines crystallized around bringing BNPL into the same consumer‑protection orbit as traditional credit, with full FCA oversight kicking in from 2026.
Add in rising delinquencies and macro headwinds, and suddenly the “approve everyone, grow at any cost” era looked a lot riskier.

How that moved GMV

The impact on GMV was more about distribution than collapse:

  • Conversion at the margin dipped in some discretionary categories.
    As providers tightened underwriting and pulled back the most aggressive “pay in 4” messaging, a slice of high‑ticket fashion, beauty, and electronics GMV that was floating on easy approvals just… didn’t happen, or happened at lower basket values.

  • GMV shifted toward “proper” credit and loyalty‑linked financing.
    Merchants with co‑branded cards, 0% promos, or tightly integrated regulated financing became relatively more attractive for big‑ticket purchases, especially where BNPL approvals were no longer automatic.

In other words: the pie didn’t disappear, but the slices got re‑cut.

How brands responded

Retailers did three things in quick succession:

  • Rationalised their BNPL panels.
    Instead of four providers jostling for real estate at checkout, many merchants now prefer one or two that play nicely with regulators and deliver sustainable economics.​

  • Re‑balanced incentives.
    Some pulled back on subsidizing BNPL promos and redirected that spend into price cuts, free shipping thresholds, or loyalty rewards that were easier to explain and defend.

  • Paid more attention to cohort behaviour.
    When cheap credit is no longer a given, you need to understand which segments genuinely need BNPL to convert and which were just using it because it was there. The former get better‑designed journeys; the latter are nudged back toward debit or cards.

How consumers responded

For shoppers, it felt like a tightening of the tap rather than a total shut‑off:

  • Some got declined more often or found limits reduced.
    Discretionary splurges became a bit less frictionless, which in turn pushed some GMV downmarket (cheaper alternatives) or out of the basket entirely

  • Others felt a bit safer.
    With clearer disclosures, better complaints mechanisms, and the knowledge that a regulator was watching, mainstream consumers were more willing to use BNPL for bigger, considered purchases.

Again, GMV didn’t vanish; it walked to whichever merchants could offer financing that felt both safe and simple under the new rules. For context, in the US, credit card debt (consumers is about $1.23TN).

Retail Media: When Shelf Space Turned Fully Pay‑to‑Play

Retail media isn’t new. What is new in 2025 is how central it has become to the P&L and how unapologetically pay‑to‑play digital shelf space now is. Large retailers and marketplaces have effectively become ad platforms with logistics operations attached. Sponsored products, branded carousels, on‑site video, off‑site targeting using first‑party data, all plugged into a measurement layer that claims to show precisely how ad spend translates into incremental GMV.

How that moved GMV

If you’re a shopper on a big marketplace, most of what you see is now, in some way, paid for:

  • GMV allocation inside those ecosystems tilted even more toward brands who could pay to win the auction for attention. Organic ranking still matters, but it is heavily shaped by sponsored demand.

  • Smaller brands, or those that refused to play the game, lost share of voice.
    Many saw their organic placement erode under waves of paid placements from better‑funded competitors, pushing their GMV into niche platforms, direct channels, or obscurity.

In practical terms: within a given marketplace, the internal GMV pie was redistributed from “best match + relevance” to “best match + relevance + who’s paying today.”

How brands responded

The budget story here is straightforward:

  • Big brands moved serious money into retail media.
    Not just test budgets; full reallocation from traditional digital and trade spend into closed‑loop, retailer‑owned inventory where they could see attributed sales and negotiate better terms.​

  • Mid‑tier players tried to hack the efficiency side.
    They leaned on better creative, smarter bidding (long‑tail keywords, defensive strategies), and joint business plans to secure programmatic visibility at lower cost.

  • Everyone started arguing about incrementality.
    The central question: “How much of this GMV would I have got anyway?” The more retail media networks could prove incremental lift, the more money flowed in.

How consumers responded

From the outside, this mostly looks like “there are a lot more sponsored things everywhere,” but underneath:

  • Some shoppers started to push back, consciously or not.
    Using filters, reviews, and, increasingly, AI agents to strip away sponsored clutter and search for “best value” or “most reliable” rather than blindly trusting the top row.

  • Others simply absorbed the new normal.
    If everything is pay‑to‑play, the path of least resistance is to lean on aggregated ratings, social proof, or brand familiarity when choosing. GMV then consolidates around whoever can win both the auction and the trust game.

Retail media turned digital shelf space from a ranking problem into a budget allocation problem. GMV followed the money. And now it is getting physical, from OOHplacements, to instore and soon to be a Vizio TV in your home. As Colin Lewis might say, everything is an ad now.

Cross‑Border Re‑Priced, Inventory Moves Closer to Home

The journey to the holy grail, Cross Border Trade/. Tariffs were the loud part of 2025’s trade story, but beneath that, logistics and geopolitical risk kept reshaping how far products travel before they hit the customer. Even where duties didn’t spike, retailers and brands saw enough disruption over the past few years, pandemics, port congestion, wars, weather, to start asking whether the last dollar of cost savings from far‑flung supply chains was really worth it.

How that moved GMV

The practical effects on GMV looked like this:

  • Fewer ultra‑slow, ultra‑cheap shipping promises.
    Retailers quietly de‑emphasised “it’ll be here in 25 days” options in favor of slightly higher‑priced but more reliable domestic or near‑shore fulfillment.

  • More conversion for those with resilient networks.
    When everyone has been burned by “your order is delayed” emails, the merchants who can promise and deliver a 2–3 day window win GMV even if they’re not the absolute cheapest.

Near‑shoring to Mexico, Eastern Europe, or domestic production doesn’t eliminate risk, but it changes the balance between cost, control, and customer trust.

How brands responded

Operationally, this is where a lot of budgets went:

  • Re‑negotiating with suppliers and moving partial production closer to key markets.

  • Investing in better inventory visibility, so the promise on the product page matches reality in the warehouse.

Narratively, some brands turned this into part of the proposition:

  • “Made closer to home,” “shorter, more transparent supply chains,” and “we’re less likely to cancel on you” became subtle but powerful messages in categories where reliability and ethics matter.

How consumers responded

For shoppers, 2025 reinforced a lesson:

  • If a deal looks too good and too far away, something might go wrong.
    Enough people experienced customs surprises, delays, or quality issues that a segment of customers simply opted for the boring, predictable option even if it cost a bit more.

GMV followed the reliable rails. The long‑tail cross‑border sellers still exist, but a meaningful slice of spend moved toward fewer, closer, more dependable nodes.

AI‑Powered Owned Sites vs Marketplace Gravity

The final story is about a fight that’s been going on for years: brand‑owned sites trying to hold onto direct relationships while marketplaces eat convenience and social platforms eat discovery. In 2025, brands finally got some better weapons. AI‑driven on‑site search, conversational assistants, and personalisation engines went from bolt‑on chat widgets to core parts of the shopping experience. Do we ever really own customers? I am Scooby dubious.

How that moved GMV

Where this was done well, the impact was real:

  • Better conversion and higher average order values on first‑party sites.
    Shoppers who might previously have bounced to Amazon for easier discovery could now ask the brand’s own assistant “show me something like the black one I bought last year, but lighter for summer,” and actually get a decent answer.

  • Shorter paths to purchase in complex categories.
    For electronics, beauty, or B2B‑ish purchases, AI assistants that could decode jargon, explain trade‑offs, and remember context made first‑party sites less painful.

That didn’t break marketplace gravity, but it slowed the leak.

How brands responded

Strategically, brands split into two camps:

  • The “everywhere our customer is” crowd:
    They accepted that a big chunk of incremental GMV would always come via marketplaces, social commerce, and agents, and invested in treating owned sites as relationship hubs rather than the only point of sale.

  • The “defensible direct” crowd:
    They doubled down on exclusive products, member perks, service‑heavy experiences, and content that you could only really get by going direct, using AI to scale the human bits rather than replace them.

Both camps invested in AI; they just framed success differently.

How consumers responded

Shoppers behaved much as you’d expect:

  • For low‑emotion buys, marketplaces still won on convenience: saved details, one cart, one app. GMV in these categories stayed highly concentrated.​

  • For higher‑stakes or more personal buys, a growing segment was willing to engage with brand‑owned AI experiences, especially when they actually solved problems instead of just mimicking a FAQ.

The result was a bifurcation of GMV: routine, replenishment, and commodity spend clustering around a handful of big ecosystems; considered, identity‑driven spend staying more distributed.

So What Do You Do With All This?

Taken together, these seven stories tell you less about “ecommerce growth” and more about “ecommerce power.” Who has the power to steer demand? Who has the power to set terms? Who has the power to absorb shocks?You need to live amongst it.

In 2025, that power shifted in a few clear directions:

  • From human choice to algorithmic mediation (agents, retail media).

  • From cross‑border arbitrage to more localised, politically palatable models (tariffs, local sellers, near‑shoring).

  • From unregulated credit sugar highs to more sustainable financing rails (BNPL regulation).

If you’re a brand or retailer planning for 2026, the practical questions to ask off the back of this year are:

  • Are we legible and attractive to the agents that will increasingly front‑run demand?

  • Do we know which parts of our GMV depend on fragile arbitrage, be it trade rules, advertising costs, or financing conditions?

  • Where are we consciously choosing to play in marketplaces, retail media, and local‑seller ecosystems, and where are we drawing lines?

  • What do we offer on our own sites that is worth bypassing the convenience of the big platforms?

Because the headline for 2025 isn’t “ecommerce grew X%.” It’s that GMV quietly re‑charted itself around new rules, new gatekeepers, and new constraints. If you’re still reading the old maps, you’ll spend next year wondering why your traffic looks fine but your checkout doesn’t.

9. Interacting: The Rise of Agentic Commerce

"Interactivity is the new narrative." — Kevin Kelly, The Inevitable

Enter agentic commerce—an ecosystem promising that every product, service, and experience will interact with us like a helpful assistant. AI-powered agents can handle customer support, answer questions, compare prices, even negotiate on our behalf. Think: chatbots, smart recommendations, virtual shopping assistants.

Everywhere you look, someone is building an agent: Shopify’s Sidekick, Amazon’s Alexa, Google’s Gemini. Agentic commerce is pitched as the next frontier—an interactive, intelligent interface between us and everything we buy.

But here’s the paradox: no consumer asked for this.

No one stood up in a focus group and said, “Please, please, make sure my entire shopping experience is driven by a bot.” Yet here we are—building, investing, and hyping these tools. Why?

Because we’re afraid. Afraid that if we don’t build them, someone else will. Afraid that we’ll miss the next big wave. Afraid that every competitor’s bot will out-sell us, out-service us, out-everything us. In this race to build agentic experiences, we’ve put the cart before the horse—assuming consumers want this, when most haven’t even decided whether they trust it.

The Unasked-for Future

Our agentic present is a mirror of our remixing past—churning out endless “intelligent” variations of the same product experience, but with more automation and less humanity.

If we use our past as a guide, history suggests we won’t adopt agentic commerce on the grand scale that technologists hope. Remember voice commerce? Touted as the next big thing, it’s still a rounding error in most companies’ revenue streams. Or personalized product recommendations? Consumers mostly skip them, either because they’re intrusive or because they simply don’t work well.

Yet, as we keep building, the real winners might not be consumers at all.

Who Really Wins in an Agentic World?

Banks, insurance companies, and healthcare providers are watching this unfold. Imagine a future where AI agents nudge us toward specific financial products, health plans, or even treatment protocols—using personalized data to “guide” us toward the right decision. On paper, it’s efficient, frictionless, even helpful.

But the reality is more complicated:

  • Insurance: AI can reward healthy behaviors—or punish risky ones—by adjusting premiums dynamically. Are we ready for a bot that tracks our gym attendance and snitches on us to our insurer?

  • Healthcare: AI agents could recommend treatments based on data, but also steer us toward cost-saving plans that benefit providers more than patients.

  • Banks: Agentic systems could manage our spending—budgeting, investing, even deciding whether we can “afford” to buy that dress. But what happens to our financial autonomy?

Our days of managing disposable income could become a BNPL bot’s domain, nudging us toward purchases that might not be in our best interest or delaying payments until we’re too deep in the cycle to escape.

A Cautionary Tale in Two Acts

Remixing and Interacting—forces eight and nine—are reshaping eCommerce in real time. They promise creativity, interactivity, and empowerment. But so far, we’ve built them because we can, not because consumers asked us to.

We need to pause and ask:

  • Are we building agentic commerce to genuinely empower consumers—or to automate our bottom lines?

  • Are we remixing to create meaning—or to churn out endless content that no one wants?

If we’re not careful, the next wave of AI-powered agents won’t be liberators of choice but gatekeepers of convenience—rewarding and punishing us in equal measure, reshaping not just what we buy but how we live.

As we move forward, let’s remember that the future isn’t inevitable. It’s built—by us, with intention, or by default.

Let’s choose wisely.

Let’s choose Life.

11. Questioning: The Power of Inquiry

“Questioning is the new answer.” — Kevin Kelly, The Inevitable

In the age of AI, one of the most fascinating developments in eCommerce is the rise of Questioning as both a technology and a mindset. From chatbots to guided search, brands are investing heavily in tools that help consumers ask questions — and, hopefully, find answers that lead to a sale.

But are chatbots the future of eCommerce, or is guided search — more structured, less robotic — a better path forward? And how does the concept of “inquiry” shape the consumer journey?

Chatbots: The Great Promise — and the Great Frustration

Chatbots have become a staple in modern eCommerce. Brands from small Shopify shops to enterprise-level giants integrate them to answer FAQs, handle returns, and recommend products. The promise is clear: 24/7 support, instant answers, lower support costs.

But chatbots can be a double-edged sword:

  • They often fail to understand context, leading to repetitive or irrelevant responses.

  • They sometimes feel like a barrier rather than a bridge, frustrating customers who just want to talk to a human.

Sure, chatbots are getting smarter with generative AI. But for many consumers, the experience still feels like talking to a souped-up FAQ rather than a helpful guide.

Guided Search: The Inquiry Path Less Travelled

Compare that with guided search, a model that prioritizes helping customers ask the right questions, and then walk them through to an answer. Think of it as a curated conversation rather than an automated monologue.

Take ThirdLove, the bra company that revolutionized lingerie shopping by reimagining the fitting process. Instead of overwhelming customers with endless SKUs, they ask a series of carefully crafted questions:

  • What’s your current size?

  • Where do your straps usually slip?

  • How does the band fit?

This “Fit Finder Quiz” isn’t a chatbot. It’s an intelligent guided search that uses inquiry to diagnose a problem (ill-fitting bras) and prescribe a solution (the right fit). The result? A personalized, confident purchase that feels tailor-made.

ThirdLove’s success proves that guided inquiry can drive conversions and build trust — customers feel heard, understood, and empowered to make the best decision.

Inquiry as a Good in Itself

Here’s the bigger picture: In a world where consumers are overwhelmed by choices and noise, the ability to ask good questions becomes a superpower. Brands that enable this — through guided search, smart surveys, interactive quizzes — are building trust and loyalty. They’re not just selling products; they’re helping customers navigate complexity.

This approach also aligns with Kevin Kelly’s idea that questioning is the new answer. In a sea of algorithms and automation, brands that lean into inquiry are saying: “We’re here to help you figure it out. We respect your needs, your preferences, and your journey.”

Should Commerce Be More About Inquiry?

Yes — and here’s why. When commerce is built around helping customers ask and answer questions, it shifts from transactional to relational. It’s not just about making a sale today, but about building a relationship where customers trust that a brand genuinely has their best interests in mind.

Brands like ThirdLove, Stitch Fix, and even IKEA with their “kitchen planner” tools, understand that inquiry isn’t just a path to revenue; it’s a path to relevance.

The Inquiry Imperative

In the race between chatbots and guided search, the winner might just be the brand that treats inquiry as a service — not a feature. Consumers don’t just want answers; they want help asking the right questions.

12. Beginning: The New Platforms

"Every new beginning comes from some other beginning's end." — Kevin Kelly, The Inevitable

We’ve spent the last decade talking about unified commerce—the idea that all touchpoints, channels, and technologies should seamlessly integrate into a single, holistic experience for customers and businesses alike. But in reality, what eCommerce leaders crave most is simpler than that: a single view of the customer and a single view of stock. Everything else is noise.

The Rise of New Platforms—and the Messy Middle

Today’s “new platforms” are reshaping the eCommerce landscape in ways both exciting and perplexing:

  • Meta and Google: Once advertising platforms, they’re evolving into semi-autonomous marketing engines, fueled by AI and machine learning. But these systems increasingly operate like black boxes: we feed them budgets and objectives, and they spit out results—often without explaining how they got there. It’s efficient, but opaque.

  • Shopify: Long celebrated for democratizing eCommerce, Shopify is now pivoting into discovery. Through Shop, they’re building a mini-marketplace that aggregates merchant products and surfaces them to customers—essentially becoming a curated browsing destination. It’s a platform within a platform, reshaping what “owning your customer” actually means.

  • Payment Providers: Companies like Stripe, Klarna, and Adyen are no longer just payments processors. They’re integrating with AI engines and data platforms to offer everything from credit risk assessment to targeted offers to checkout optimization. Payments are now a node in the commerce ecosystem, not just an endpoint.

The Connected Future—or Just More Complexity?

These new platforms are deeply interconnected:

  • Shopify plugs into Meta and Google.

  • Payment providers plug into Shopify, Amazon, and countless others.

  • AI engines from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are weaving themselves into customer support, content, and even product design.

On paper, this interconnectedness promises seamless commerce: every piece of the puzzle—ads, stock, payments, returns—working in harmony. But in reality, it can feel like platform soup. Each platform wants to be the “hub” while everything else orbits around it. But that leaves merchants stuck with ever-expanding tech stacks, each promising unification but delivering even more silos.

The Tech Stack Conundrum

Every new platform brings a promise: plug in, turn on, get results. But every new integration also adds a new layer of complexity:

  • Data Fragmentation: The more platforms we connect, the more we risk duplicating customer records, product data, and reporting metrics.

  • Black Box Marketing: As Meta and Google automate more of our marketing, we risk losing visibility into what’s actually driving results—and how to optimize spend responsibly.

  • Stock and Customer View: The golden goose of eCommerce remains elusive—a single, real-time view of inventory across all channels and a single, comprehensive profile of each customer.

In this environment, the biggest winners might be the platforms that can reduce complexity, provide clarity, and empower merchants to make sense of it all.

Is This Why Shopify Keeps Winning?

Shopify’s strategy of continuous iteration—Becoming—might be its biggest strength. It’s not trying to be the entire internet; it’s trying to be the most merchant-centric commerce platform. By focusing on merchant experiences and iterating fast (think Shopify Editions), Shopify remains agile while Amazon increasingly looks like a one-size-fits-all marketplace. In the race to build the best tech stack, Shopify’s “Start here, grow with us” approach is winning hearts—and wallets.

Trent: Doesn't that suck?

Mike: Why'd they get rid of the fighting? It was the best part of the old version.

Sue: I think kids were hittin' each other or somethin', man.

Trent: Yeah but you know what, Mike? You can make their heads bleed in this one.

Mike: Make somebody's head bleed.

Sue: No man, we're in the playoffs.

Something has bothered me for some time and I wanted to try piece this together about 6 months ago. I started and then I stopped. US conferences are littered with people my age and older. UK I am the old guy. The stories are being delivered by completely different people. It’s not just an age or culture thing. It is to do with how companies are owned and structured. Dig a little deeper off the conference circuit and you will find them. Maybe.

For a solid decade, building a DTC brand felt like the ecommerce equivalent of counting cards. You needed cheap capital, a Shopify store, and a decent founder origin story. Thanks to the ZIRP years (Zero Interest Rate Policy, 2008–2021), capital was effectively free, VC firms were swimming in dry powder, and the barrier to entry was low — but the ceiling was sky high - said Icarus.

Between 2014 and 2021, over 85 DTC brands achieved unicorn status globally (Oh how I dreamt of it - fact check, I actually dreamt of this last Thursday. Spawning the need to continue the article - sad bat*ard) — many with Millennial founders at the helm. US and UK names like Glossier, Casper, Away, Allbirds, BrewDog (I am an unofficial shareholder - drink consumptionO , Made.com, and Gymshark all raised at high multiples on the back of direct-to-consumer hype, investor FOMO, and CAC-fueled growth.

But here’s the kicker: most of them underperformed post-2021.

  • Casper went public in 2020, then was taken private for a fraction of its IPO value.

  • Made.com collapsed into administration in 2022.

  • Allbirds stock is down over 95% from IPO peak.

  • Glossier laid off staff and pivoted to wholesale with Sephora.

In hindsight, many of these brands weren’t built to last — they were built to scale. Growth was the KPI. Profit was optional. It worked while interest rates were near zero and Facebook ROAS was still above water.Today it is still above water, just, and is still a barometer of survival for many.

Then the music stopped.You and me and a bottle make three tonight.

Enter Gen Z — a generation raised in the ashes of Millennial ecommerce ambition, hardened by recessions, algorithms, and economic chaos. Their playbook doesn’t start with a seed round. It starts with a phone, an idea, and a comment section. The phone, arguably if the iPhone were not invented, I would not be writing this.

I wante to explore for some time how Gen Z brand builders are approaching the game differently — and what legacy, if any, Millennial DTC culture has left behind.

Because in 2025, it’s not about whether you’re “so money.”
It’s whether you know how to turn attention into margin. “What do I do with these fangs? How do I kill the bunny?”

While Millennial DTCs rode the wave of cheap money and predictable media buying, the post-2019 era has looked radically different. Gen Z-founded or Gen Z-aligned brands emerged in a world where:

  • Paid media no longer guaranteed predictable growth. It did once upon a time.

  • Consumers demanded transparency, ethics, and entertainment

  • And funding came with strings, dilution, or… just didn’t come at all. This is an almost daily cautionary tale in the news.

But here's a twist: they’re growing anyway — and sometimes, faster.

Since 2019, a new cohort of DTC challengers has gained traction not by outspending competitors, but by out-creating and out-connecting with their audiences.

Notable post-2019 Gen Z-era DTC brands:

Many of these brands were bootstrapped or launched with micro-funding, and grew through creator partnerships, community-building, and channel-native storytelling. They seem to know where there audiences are because the are their own consumer first. Not square pegged into a round hole.

Unlike the ZIRP-era unicorns, they don’t need $50 million to break through — they need a viral moment, a smart creator collab, and a shipping partner that can handle scale.

What’s more? These brands often report profitability within 12–24 months, not because they’re cautious, but because they’re building for cash flow, not burn rate. This is something I learned alot about recently - - It didn’t occur to me for sometime.

There is a fluency around the speech of cash flow in this world that is not spoken about.

So if the Millennial era of DTC was about scale, sleekness, and Series B...The Gen Z era is about scrappiness, story, and soul.

These brands aren’t just selling smells, sunscreen, sweats, or serums — they’re building identities. Movements. Micro-tribes. In fact, if Millennial DTC was a business plan with a vibe layered on top, Gen Z DTC is a vibe with a business model wrapped around it.

Note: Gymsahrk Head of Brand Noel Mack articulates their COVID story so well. Careful social listening meant their community thrived and expanded during COVID. It gave them licence to appear elsewhere and move from Gym Floors to Front Rooms and then into Yoga Studios - now they boast stores in London and New York.

Djerf Avenue. It doesn’t run ads. It barely uses traditional influencers. Yet it has built one of the most loyal, global customer bases in fashion — Every post, drop, and caption is in her voice. The comments section reads like a group chat. The fans don’t just wear the clothes — they evangelize the ethos.

Or look at Topicals, the skincare brand founded by Olamide Olowe. Topicals isn’t selling you perfect skin — it’s selling you self-acceptance, community care, and science-backed honesty. The brand’s most viral campaigns have come not from influencers, but from raw, heartfelt stories shared by its own customers. Many try to repeat this formula, many fail.

And Youthforia, built on the idea that makeup should be safe enough to sleep in, built its early community on TikTok not with polished UGC, but by showing founder Fiona Co Chan experimenting with formulations, answering DMs, and turning skincare routines into storytelling formats.

So here’s my question:

Do Gen Z founders simply understand social media — and by extension, modern culture — in a more instinctive, authentic way than their Millennial predecessors?

The evidence suggests yes. Not always in structured case studies, but in the thousands of micro-interactions that happen daily:

  • Founders replying to DMs directly

  • TikToks made on the fly that outperform six-figure campaign shoots

  • Discords, BeReals, Close Friends stories — not for press, but for proximity

  • Product lines and drops co-created in comment sections, not market research decks

What used to be called "community" is now embedded into the product, the packaging, the pitch decks. And in this world, community isn’t something you build — it’s something you belong to.

It’s not that Millennials didn’t try to do this..

They live in the algorithm. They are the algorithm.

Hang On Voltaire

And yet, not all Millennial-led brands followed the same script of heavy paid ads, cool packaging, and eventual burnout. Some — like Fanatics — quietly built something far more resilient: an ecosystem. (Oft repeated, rarely replicated).

Founded by Michael Rubin, a Millennial entrepreneur with a long history in commerce, Fanatics didn’t chase DTC hype. Instead, it built a digital empire by embedding itself directly into the infrastructure of sports fandomnot just through merchandise, but through partnerships, licensing, and platform control.

In many ways, Fanatics is the ultimate Millennial-led platform play:

  • It owns the rights to produce and distribute official merchandise for leagues like the NFL, NBA, and Premier League.

  • It partners with media companies, sportsbooks, and even NFT platforms.

  • It’s vertically integrated to the point that Fanatics can design, manufacture, sell, and ship product — often within hours of a major game or viral moment.

It’s relentlessly fan-first.

From limited edition drops timed to real-world sports events to customization that puts the buyer in control, Fanatics operates like a SaaS company that happens to sell jerseys. The data loop is tight. The brand loyalty is tribal. And the experience is built not just for the moment of purchase but for a lifetime of fandom.

Fanatics shows us that Millennial brands — when built with infrastructure, partnerships, and purpose — can scale culture in a different but equally powerful way.

Fanatics isn’t trying to be relatable. It’s trying to be inevitable.

Now to look at what has happened and what is happening. A potted reflection.

Platforms, Tech & Channels

“This place is dead anyway.” – Trent

The first sign of a generational shift? What they build on — and more importantly, what they don’t.

Millennials built DTC empires with Shopify, Klaviyo, and Facebook Ads. It was a predictable stack: plug, play, scale. Agencies were hired, LTVs were calculated, and growth loops were baked in with surgical precision. It was chess.

But Gen Z is playing Fortnite. They’re skipping full tech stacks in favor of social-first, scrappy, and wildly dynamic go-to-market moves. To them, Shopify is optional. Virality is not. And when Shopify does enter the picture, it’s often after they’ve already proven traction via TikTok Shop, live drops, or Discord pre-orders. (It is not all healthy or a world I want, but)

US Examples:

  • Glossier had a blog, a waitlist, and VC money.

  • Finesse uses AI to decide what to design next — flipping the product pipeline upside down.

UK Examples:

  • TALA launched on third-party systems before replatforming at scale — now a Shopify Plus brand, but only once the foundations were proven. (Grace Beverley, Founder spoke at eComm Live in Belfast a month ago. She is an incredible proponent of this lifestyle). Lifestyle and smarts. WOW.

What’s going on here?

There’s a potential correlation that’s worth considering:
Gen Z brands may be consciously or unconsciously delaying major tech investments to prioritize the right people, not just the right platform. People grow communities remember.

While Millennials often secured VC early and raced to build scalable infrastructure (internal ops, robust ecommerce stacks, 3PLs), Gen Z seems more inclined to:

  • Outsource ops early via scrappy tools or freelancers.

  • Focus in-house talent on brand, storytelling, and community.

  • Keep overhead light and decision-making nimble.

Instead of hiring a VP of Ops in month two, Gen Z founders are hiring a content editor or a community manager. Their first five hires might include a TikTok creator, a Discord mod (Yes, I have a Discord account), and someone who “just gets memes.” And weirdly, it works.

In the old DTC world, tech was the enabler. In the new one, tech is background noise — people and proximity are the differentiators.

If the Millennial ecommerce stack was a paint-by-numbers mural. Gen Z prefers graffiti — temporary, viral, and designed to get you talking. And maybe, by holding off on tech-heavy investments, they’re giving themselves the budgetary and creative space to build something more emotionally scalable: a real community.

Hiring & Team Culture

“You’re growin’, you’re learnin’, and I’m the one who’s gettin’ better.” – Mike

If at first is about what you build with, this phase is about who you build with — and how long they stick around. Leaving is not a bad sign. There seems to be role and brand fluidity. You learn at one place and someone else benefits. Contracts are changing, as are roles.

Millennials Built Teams to Scale

Millennial DTC brands followed a well-trodden hiring path:

  • Seed round → hire a Head of Growth

  • Series A → bring in a VP of Ops, a Head of Brand, and a Retention Lead

  • Series B → stack out the org chart like you’re building a LinkedIn B2B SaaS company

Tenure mattered. Roles were clearly defined. You wanted the person who’d “been at Warby” or “scaled something from $5M to $50M.” The same faces, from the same LinkedIn carousel, doing the same job at the next funded startup.

There was safety in pattern-matching — even when that pattern led to bloated orgs and internal turf wars by year three. Hoping I get picked up for something soon BTW - price for anyone noticing this.

Gen Z Hires In Platform, Not In Theory

Gen Z founders think about experience differently — and not just because they haven’t had time to build ten years of it themselves.

They want:

  • People who live inside the platform.

  • People who get the joke before it's explained.

  • People who can react in real time, not run a four-week sprint retrospective.

In this world, a 21-year-old TikTok mod with three years of content-native instinct may be more valuable than a 35-year-old CMO with a polished resume and a PowerPoint deck on Gen Z behavior.

Roles are fluid. Job descriptions are vibes. Titles might be “Head of Chaos,” “Moodboard Ops,” or “Community Wizard.” The structure is secondary to the energy. I know we shake our heads and say WTAF. (Why the face - Phil Dunphy).

Tenure? It’s Not the Point

It’s increasingly common in Gen Z-led teams to see people cycle in and out within 12–18 months. Not because of burnout or toxicity — but because the job evolves too fast for the org structure to keep up. Platforms, algos change - behaviors that change are more micro than macro - maybe my single biggest learning here.

Freelancers become co-founders. Creators become merch managers. A Discord community lead might disappear one day… and pop back up six months later with a whole new idea.

Gen Z leadership understands that team loyalty isn’t measured in years — it’s measured in impact velocity. The question isn’t “How long will you stay?” It’s “What can you help us do right now?”

Key Contrast: The Hiring Compass

If Millennial founders hired for predictability, Gen Z hires for presence. It’s not about your resume — it’s about your reaction time in the group chat. And in this new era, loyalty isn’t proven in performance reviews. It’s shown by dropping the right gif at the right time. With my GIF volume I think I am regressing - more on that later.

Always Double Down on 11: Funding

For Millennial DTC brands, venture capital wasn't just a funding option — it was the default OS. Between 2010 and 2020, the direct-to-consumer boom was fueled by a flood of VC and private equity money. Globally, DTC startups raised between $8 billion to $10 billion across more than 600 deals since the start of 2019 alone .

This capital influx was driven by the promise of rapid growth and the allure of disrupting traditional retail models. Brands like Glossier, Casper, and Allbirds became emblematic of this era, securing massive funding rounds to scale operations, invest in customer acquisition, and expand product lines.

Growth-at-all-costs mentality often led to unsustainable business practices. Many of these brands faced challenges in achieving profitability, with high customer acquisition costs and intense competition eroding margins. The pressure to deliver quick returns to investors sometimes resulted in strategic missteps and overexpansion. In many cases the model for growth adopted was the ones the money wanted to see. They thought they had it right. UK finance was more risk led and didn’t see the same path forward much to my own frustration with Crua. Valuations were smaller, equity requests higher and dilution was not just a popular Irish summer drink.

In contrast, Gen Z entrepreneurs are approaching funding with a different mindset. They prioritize sustainable growth, community engagement, and authentic brand storytelling over rapid scaling. Many are opting for alternative funding methods, such as crowdfunding, bootstrapping, or seeking smaller, strategic investments that align with their brand values.

This shift reflects a broader change in the entrepreneurial landscape, where success is measured not just by valuation or market share, but by the strength of the community built around a brand and its long-term impact.

“It’s not so much me as it is Roenick; he’s good.” – Mike (after losing at NHL '94)

Millennials were the VC darlings. Their brands were in pitch decks from Soho House to Silicon Valley. They raised big rounds, burned cash to acquire users, and aimed for acquisition or IPO. That strategy built unicorns and also some very public faceplants.How do we spend all this money?

Gen Z watched that play out and said, “Nah, we’re good.” Instead, they crowdfund, pre-sell, and bootstrap. If they take capital, it’s often from non-traditional sources — creator funds, community-driven DAOs, or low-dilution indie VCs.

Crowdfunding is something I have worked in for 8 years + and it speaks the same language as GEn Z. Kickstarter is all about community building, common purpose and belief in purpose over certainty. Seedrs, a testament to ingenuity and people wanting to belong. More on that in a retrospective.

Millennial Wins:

  • Bloom & Wild → Big PE backing (They really piss off my Irish client who is a competior)

  • Casper → IPO with major buzz

  • Outdoor Voices → Raised millions, built a vibe (until it imploded)

Gen Z Moves:

  • Djerf Avenue → Bootstrapped, insanely profitable

  • Feastables → Launched via MrBeast's content engine

  • Youthforia → Landed in Target without VC hype

For Millennials, capital was fuel. For Gen Z, it’s seasoning. A little goes a long way and too much ruins the dish.

It’s Scorcese, Everything is Derivative: Culture & Values

“I don’t want you to be the guy in the PG-13 movie everyone’s really hoping makes it.” – Trent

Culture isn’t what’s on the About page — it’s how the brand behaves when no one’s watching.

Millennials injected sustainability and inclusivity into their brands after the Series A. It was a move toward relevance, not always belief. Gen Z? They start with their identity. If the brand isn’t value-driven from day one, they won’t build it and consumers won’t trust it. That’s why Costner did so well. An early believer in himself.

Whether it’s mental health transparency, LGBTQ+ support, or anti-fast-fashion supply chains, Gen Z brands reflect who they are, not just what they sell. This will become even more impotant as DEI is being eroded on the high street. Brand values will be sought out and this is a place where Agentic commerce could find a way forward. Cater only to my beliefs, forget the rest.

Case in Point:

  • Gen Z brands shut down for mental health days — and post about it. I sometimes cringe seeing some of it. But just be around these people, they believe. It is hard not to feel inspired or silly in equal measure. Silly, for reference in that I am a generation removed.

  • Their "About Us" pages read like diary entries.Dog Days Diaries, i mean…

  • They actively dismantle DTC norms: size charts, return policies, even packaging.

If Millennials tried to look good on paper, Gen Z is more concerned with how they look crying on TikTok. Vulnerability isn’t a weakness it’s the content plan.

Category Winners & Losers

“This is a gorgeous baby. You’re money. You’re so money and you don’t even know it.” – Trent

Some categories lend themselves to generational reinvention — others cling to the old guard.

Gen Z Success Categories

Gen Z owns the impulse buy. Millennials still rule the considered purchase. But watch closely even furniture might go viral in the right hands (hello, TikTok couches).

Hang on Voltaire: The Generational Face-Off

“I don’t want to be one of those ex-suit guys sitting in a coffee shop.” – Mike

I’ll be honest — classifying generations is messy business. Nobody wakes up and says, “I’m building like a textbook Millennial today,” or “Time to lead with full Gen Z energy.” Reality is blurrier than that. What you’ll read here isn’t carved in stone. It’s not a McKinsey quadrant. Thankfully. It’s a pattern — one I’ve noticed after years working with DTC founders, speaking at events, watching pitch decks roll in, and sharing drinks with both exhausted CMOs and hyper-energized 22-year-olds who can build a cult following in a weekend.

Some brands straddle generations. Some teams are run by a Millennial founder with a Gen Z brain trust. Some Gen Z brands will raise $50M and blow it. Some Millennial brands will pivot, downsize, and finally find sustainable profit in year seven. There are no hard and fast rules — only shifting energies, different tools, and evolving instincts.I like to think this is something to watch. Particularly as I find myself increasingly looking to get back into brand world. Where do I fit? I should be employable, but am I? Really?

Because whether you’re building your brand off vibes or venture debt, one thing’s certain: ecommerce is no longer a one-size-fits-all game. As I said before we operate in a multi tiered system.

Trait

This isn’t a passing of the torch — it’s a burning of the playbooks. Gen Z didn’t wait for permission to lead and they don’t ask for forgiveness. They just turned the camera on and started talking.

This my friends, is breakfast in the Age of Enlightenment.

IYKYK.

“We Don’t Want to Be Tracked. We Want to Be Recognized.”

Start With the Dinosaur Dig

Let’s begin with dinosaurs.

Not the stale, fossilized kind of marketing thinking that refuses to evolve. I’m talking about actual dinosaurs, specifically, the ones Dave Finnegan spent his summer digging up in Portugal.

When Dave joined us on The Watson Weekend, he didn’t just come with stories of CMOs and brand playbooks. He came with dirt still under his fingernails. And a story true, scientifically valid, and metaphorically juicy that has been an inner ear worm for me since. (It has only been 72 hours) but we pre recorded and I was privy to what has was going to share. So this has been a long time in the making.

While on-site with a team from the Natural History Museum, Dave learned how the inner ear of a creature can tell you everything: whether it was cold-blooded or warm-blooded, agile or sluggish, predator or prey.

And most mind-blowingly of all, how, about 233 million years ago, a rainstorm that lasted two million years (yes, seriously) led to a climate so wildly transformative that it literally rewired evolution. Warm-bloodedness emerged. Dinosaurs took over.

Why? Because the ear evolved.
Because sensing, adapting, and responding became the dominant survival advantage.

Now hold that thought.

Curiosity and the Inner Ear of Commerce

A few weeks ago, I wrote this on LinkedIn:

"Culture > KPIs. Why curiosity could be your most underrated marketing metric."

It resonated. Said the egotistical consultant. In the sea of AI hacks, attribution wars, and cookie banner fatigue, the simple act of wondering again of feeling, listening, asking why feels increasingly rare. If we as marketers are to be curious, we as consumers want to be reconigzed. We willingly leave clues and signals, only largely to be ignored. What disservice this must be doing to our industry. Not recognizing the evolutionary path we are on. Nick Kaplan describes this period as Darwinian and it is not to sound dramatic or draconian, it is wayu worse than that. The dinosaurs taught us anything, it's that evolution doesn’t reward dominance it rewards responsiveness.

And that’s where Dave dropped another truth bomb:

"Customers don’t want to be tracked. They want to be recognized."

Let that sit for a moment.

In just 10 words, Dave obliterated half the martech industry’s value proposition. He reframed a decade of digital surveillance as a failure of imagination. We didn’t build tech wrong because of what it does we built it wrong because of what we called it.

Recognition, not tracking.
Belonging, not personalization.
Meaning, not metrics.

Words matter. And we’ve been using the wrong ones.

Anthropology > Attribution

As I mentioned earlier, Dave isn’t your typical CMO. He’s an anthropologist. An actual, studying-the-human-condition, bone-dust-on-his-shoes anthropologist. And that lens—that ability to see not just what people do but why they do it—is where his marketing philosophy stands apart. He shared that hs is on a course to study one new chapter a month, for life. A telling statement but said with the absolute satisfaction of someone who finds this vocational. I imagine marketing to him, is easy, understanding behaviors is fun and interesting. Dave is curious.

Anthropology, as he reminded us, is the pursuit of meaning over measurement. It's not enough to know the click-through rate; we need to know why they clicked. Or didn’t. Or rage-closed the tab and wrote a passive-aggressive tweet. This is a way better articulation of curiosity as a KPI.

Dave pointed out that we’re so obsessed with optimizing journeys and reducing friction, we’ve forgotten the thing that makes any journey worth taking: connection.

In a world full of personalization engines and AI-generated emails, what people actually crave isn’t another funnel nudge, it’s a moment that makes them feel seen. I have worked on this idea of moments for years now. Moments win marketing and retailing and trading is now about winning the day, not the week or the month. We wake up to win every day. This, right now, is exhausting. This, is not, going away.

Dave told a story about a Build-A-Bear experience where a 10-year-old girl born into iPads and TikTok lit up not because of a digital interaction, but because someone in-store recognized it was her birthday and called the whole team over to sing. We sometimes think of these experiences and cringe. Maybe we have forgotten that in those cringe moments a little bit of joy is exposed inside us or desire or longing.

The metric? Off the charts.
The meaning? Even better.

For everything else, there’s (I won’t don’t worry.)

Tech’s Language Problem

Which brings me back to the language.

Tracking. Optimizing. Capturing. Converting.

We’ve built the entire modern marketing stack around words borrowed from surveillance, warfare, and mechanical engineering. Is it any wonder consumers feel like lab rats being A/B tested into submission? Maybe this is the Amazon effect at its most effective.

Dave’s quote is a full system override. It offers a new vocabulary for an industry badly in need of one:

This isn’t just semantics. It’s strategy.

Here’s the paradox we must embrace:

Consumers want privacy, but they also want relevance.
 They fear being watched, but love being known.

I think this is what it must feel like to be French. :)

And if that feels contradictory, congratulations you’re officially in the business of being human.

What the Data Actually Says

Plenty of studies back this up. I wanted to try and validate myself. Usually a glance in the mirror does that (You are old O Brien, get over it).

According to McKinsey, 71% of consumers expect personalization, and 76% get frustrated when they don’t find it. Yet simultaneously, 86% say data privacy is a growing concern.

So how do we reconcile this?

The answer isn’t more data. It’s better intent. Recognition over reduction. Understanding over optimization.

People are saying:

  • “Don’t scrape me. See me.”

  • “Don’t follow me. Welcome me.”

  • “Don’t infer what I want. Ask me.”

Behavioral economist Rory Sutherland once said: “A change in perspective is worth 80 IQ points.”
Well, a change in language might be worth a hundred brand points. Possibly more. And no one argues with Rory.

What If We’ve Been Building It All Wrong?

The reason this poiece took so long was that the real kicker in Dave’s insight is this: it’s not just marketing language that’s broken It’s the architecture that follows it.

When I think about it, it feels like this. If you start with “How do I track them?” You build a system optimized for consent forms, cookies, and opt-outs. (Slow down Jon, I know you are going to jump on this.)
If you start with “How do I recognize them?”
You build something completely different—something that might even feel... hospitable.

Recognition opens the door to:

  • Identity without intrusion.

  • Loyalty without bribery.

  • Experience without surveillance.

It's not just more ethical. It's more effective. It is also language that can help us, as consumers, retrain our own expectations of what we want. We have come to expect things without thinking. We have become passive in our own interactions in most things we do. Thanks Social Media.

AI, Meaning, and the New Power Structure

One of Dave’s other mic-drop moments on the show was this:

“AI is shifting the power structure. It’s the Gutenberg press moment of our era.”

The printing press moved power from the few (clergy, kings, scholars) to the many (readers, writers, rebels). AI is doing the same putting expert-level tools in everyone’s pocket. I am still struggling with what is in front of us, AI wise and also why it is here at all. Having these tools to be effective for us will require expert level curiosity to match the tools. OTherwise we won’t’ realize their value.

But with great power comes... well, some really awful prompts. Let’s be honest. Oh Spiderman, you appear everywhere.

So the brands that win won’t be the ones with the most AI. They’ll be the ones who apply it with empathy.

They’ll use AI to amplify empathy, not automate it.

That means:

  • Using data to make a customer feel seen, not segmented.

  • Using personalization to create a sense of belonging, not behavioral nudges.

  • Using AI to tell better stories, not faster spam.

The realization in the writing is that this will take time. As everything else speeds up, for the most community building slows down. Community was the other word mentioned. Community building takes time, effort and energy, something we fail to grasp. And time is a thief, it has been now for a decade, robbing us of our ability to be bored, engaged or interested all at the same time and instead forcing us to fill it with so called experiences and self improvement. When did we stop being happy progressing slowly. 1 class a month for life seems like a nice pace to me.

Belonging Beats Personalization

Dave also called out something we rarely talk about:

“Personalization is overrated. Belonging is the thing we’re really after.”

Boom.

We obsess over predictive algorithms and recommendation engines, and forget that the ultimate recommendation is community. People want to see themselves reflected in a brand—not just through a product recommendation, but through values, language, and cultural fluency.

If personalization is transactional, belonging is transformational.Belonging is another way to describe community. When we glibly talk about it at conferences we never describe the rate or scale of belonging our communities feel with us.

The Rituals We Forgot

Another insight: marketers used to understand ritual. Not in the performative, content-calendar sense but as a form of shared meaning.

Think about how Build-A-Bear turns a birthday into a production. Not every brand can do this, but then if a brand has no real purpose for being …. Or how Yeti doesn’t sell coolers they sell a rugged, slow-smoked ideal of life. In a test for Yeti, my team and I once stored ice in our Tundra 400 and after 23 days, we still had ice. The beers were gone, but the ice remained. Or how Arc’teryx designs half-theater, half-retail environments to tell stories of wind-swept summits, not SKUs.

These brands didn’t just sell stuff. They created clubs.

Dave shared this:

“A brand is a club you want to belong to.”

And clubs have rituals.
Rituals have meaning.
Meaning makes money.

Rituals are always a part of the daily routine. If you can get into routine to be ritualistic or habitual, maybe you have a shot. This is, in large part, why Shopify do so well in the tech world. They are routine, their sales process is too. It is part of how agencies acr, talk, sell and hunt. All bound by this sense of belonging.

My Takeaways

Let’s land this heilcopter. Here’s what Dave Finnegan taught me—and hopefully, now you too:

  • Words matter. “Track” vs. “recognize” changes everything.

  • Empathy is an action, not a vibe. Investigate, don’t just guess. (vibe, sorry Rick. It’s everywhere. I blame you.)

  • Belonging > Personalization. Sell community, not segmentation.

  • AI is not the point. It’s the amplifier. Use it wisely.

  • Recognition is a new strategic lever. Build for mirrors, not megaphones.

And most of all?

Be the inner ear.
Sense what’s changing. Evolve.
Find your warm-blooded moment—and run with it.

Thank You, Dave

For bringing anthropology, humanity, and an archaeologist’s chisel to the often plastic world of marketing. For reminding us that people want to be felt, not filed.

You gave us more than a quote.

You gave us a new language.

Let’s hope we’re smart enough to use it.

Now, over to you...

  • Are you building for tracking or recognition?

  • What brand made you feel seen recently? This is hard and maybe not always the purpose.

  • What’s a better marketing word we should all adopt?

Drop it in the comments. I’m listening. And I’m curious.
